- **[T1-]** Aelian repeatedly wrote about Alexander (356–323 BCE), including his demand for divine honours, dealings with philosophers, treatment of companions, and campaigns in Asia. Aelian composed these retrospective anecdotes in the Roman Empire roughly five centuries later. **Documented fact** that Aelian wrote about Alexander; individual anecdotes vary in historical reliability ([*Varia historia* 1.25; 2.19](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist2.html), [3.23](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist3.html), [12.54](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist12.html)).

- **[T3]** Aelian engaged extensively with Aristotle’s writings and biographical tradition. *On Animals* adopts, paraphrases, contests, and supplements Aristotelian zoological material, while *Varia historia* recounts episodes involving Aristotle, including his relations with Plato and Alexander. **Documented fact** of one-sided written engagement; dependence in particular animal passages may involve intermediary compilations rather than direct consultation of complete Aristotelian texts ([*Varia historia* 3.19; 4.9, 4.19](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist4.html); [Aelian animal-text index and translations](https://www.attalus.org/info/aelian.html)).

- **[T3]** Aelian explicitly names and evaluates Ctesias as an authority for Persian and Indian marvels, most conspicuously the manticore. His qualifying formula—accepting the report only if Ctesias is a sufficient authority—constitutes direct one-sided textual engagement with a writer active around the late fifth and early fourth centuries BCE. **Documented fact**, although whether Aelian read Ctesias directly or through excerpts is unresolved ([*On Animals* 4.21](https://topostext.org/work/560); [*Encyclopaedia Iranica*, “Aelianus, Claudius”](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aelianus-claudius/)).

- **[T3]** Aelian identifies Megasthenes, the Hellenistic envoy and author of an *Indica* (active around 300 BCE), as an authority for Indian fauna and peoples. The relationship is textual and separated by roughly five centuries; direct use of the complete *Indica*, rather than an epitome or intermediary source, cannot be demonstrated. **Documented fact** of citation and reuse; exact transmission route uncertain ([*On Animals*, searchable complete text](https://topostext.org/work/560); [*Encyclopaedia Iranica*](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aelianus-claudius/)).

- **[T3]** Aelian repeatedly quotes, paraphrases, and disputes Homeric animal lore and myth—for example contrasting Homer’s Chimaera with the allegedly natural amphisbaena. This is one-sided literary engagement with the Homeric poems, not evidence concerning a historical meeting or even Homer’s personal historicity. **Documented fact** ([*On Animals* 9.23](https://topostext.org/work/560); [chapter index](https://www.attalus.org/info/aelian.html)).

- **[T3]** Aelian cites and discusses verses and traditions attributed to Hesiod, treating the poet as an inherited authority while occasionally comparing competing accounts. **Documented fact** of one-sided textual engagement; claims about Hesiod’s life transmitted by Aelian remain ancient literary tradition rather than independently verified biography ([*Varia historia* 3.18](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist3.html), [13.19](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist13.html)).

- **[T3]** Aelian engages with Herodotus both as a stylistic-historical predecessor and as a transmitter of ethnographic and animal material. He also reports biographical and reception anecdotes about Herodotus. **Documented fact** of one-sided written engagement; agreement between the authors does not always establish direct borrowing because intermediary compilations are possible ([*Varia historia* 4.21](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist4.html), [13.20](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist13.html)).

- **[T1-]** Aelian made Plato (died 348/347 BCE) a recurring subject of *Varia historia*, relating anecdotes about his habits, humility, pupils, travels, philosophical rivalries, and reception. These are retrospective literary notices written approximately five and a half centuries later. **Documented fact** that Aelian wrote about Plato; the historicity of individual anecdotes is variable ([*Varia historia* 2.18](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist2.html), [3.17](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist3.html), [4.9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist4.html)).

- **[T1-]** Aelian preserves sayings and character anecdotes attributed to Diogenes the Cynic (fourth century BCE), including material concerning his contempt for conventional status and his judgments of other Greeks. **Documented fact** that Aelian wrote about the earlier philosopher; particular sayings are **reported facts** within the ancient anecdotal tradition, not independently verified utterances ([*Varia historia* 3.29](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist3.html), [12.58](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist12.html)).

- **[T1-]** Aelian wrote retrospective stories about Cyrus II of Persia (died c. 530 BCE), including his upbringing, character, royal conduct, and treatment of subjects. **Documented fact** that Cyrus appears in Aelian’s historical miscellany; the episodes themselves are **reported facts or literary traditions**, sometimes complicated by the existence of Cyrus the Younger in other Aelian passages ([*Varia historia* 1.24](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist1.html), [12.42](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist12.html)).

- **[T1-]** In *On Animals* 9.61 Aelian discusses the tradition that Cleopatra VII (69–30 BCE) died through the bite of an asp, treating animal behaviour as evidence bearing on the reported manner of her death. **Documented fact** that Aelian wrote about Cleopatra; death by deliberately applied snakebite is a **reported fact/disputed historical tradition**, not something Aelian could have witnessed ([*On Animals* 9.61](https://topostext.org/work/560); [Attalus ancient-source index for Cleopatra](https://www.attalus.org/names/c/cleopatra.html)).

- **[T1-]** Aelian preserves biographical and legendary notices about Pindar (c. 518–c. 438 BCE), including the story of bees placing honey on the sleeping poet’s lips and traditions concerning honours paid to him. **Documented fact** that Aelian wrote about Pindar; the honey episode is **rumor or myth**, functioning as a conventional sign of divinely favoured eloquence ([*Varia historia* 12.45](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist12.html), [13.25](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist13.html)).

- **[T1-]** Aelian recounts sayings and biographical anecdotes concerning Simonides (c. 556–468 BCE), particularly traditions about money, patrons, memory, and poetic conduct. **Documented fact** that Aelian wrote about Simonides; the individual episodes are **reported facts** from the ancient anecdotal tradition ([*Varia historia* 9.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist9.html), [10.2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist10.html)).

- **[T1-]** Aelian retells material concerning Odysseus—listed in the roster as Ulysses—especially animal-related episodes grounded in Homeric tradition, including the fidelity and recognition associated with his dog Argus. **Documented fact** that Aelian wrote about the literary figure; the underlying events are **rumor or myth**, not historical biography ([*On Animals*, complete searchable text](https://topostext.org/work/560); [chapter index](https://www.attalus.org/info/aelian.html)).

- **[T1-]** Aelian reports a Greek biographical tradition that Zoroaster was exceptionally wise and records claims about his antiquity. Since Aelian wrote centuries after the period to which Greek writers assigned Zoroaster, this is a retrospective literary connection only. **Documented fact** that Aelian transmitted the notice; its chronological and biographical content is **reported fact or legend**, not securely recoverable history ([Aelian fragments, with source cross-references](https://www.attalus.org/translate/aelian_f1.html)).

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** In the second–third centuries CE, Aelian repeatedly named Megasthenes as an authority on Indian animals. One surviving passage attributes to him reports of immense winged scorpions and nocturnal winged snakes, illustrating Aelian’s role in preserving—and sometimes amplifying—the *Indika*’s natural-history tradition. [Aelian, *On Animals* 16.41](https://www.attalus.org/translate/animals16.html)
Aelian later transmitted literary anecdotes and traditions concerning figures from the Hannibalic world.

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** While Cleopatra resided at Caesar’s gardens in Rome in 46–44 BCE, Cicero dealt with her court over promised scholarly materials and later described the queen’s *superbia* (“arrogance”) and her agent Ammonius in a contemporary letter to Atticus dated June 44 BCE. The surviving evidence establishes one-sided written engagement and direct dealings with her household, but does not securely document a private meeting between them. [Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* 15.15](https://www.attalus.org/cicero/atticus15.html)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact (literary reception):** More than thirteen centuries after Cleopatra’s death, Dante placed her among the lustful in the second circle of Hell in *Inferno* V, composed in the early fourteenth century. His characterization belongs to the medieval moralizing tradition and is not independent historical evidence about her life. [Dante, *Inferno*, Canto V](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/1001/1001-h/1001-h.htm)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact (later historiography containing allegations):** Writing in the late first century CE, Josephus discussed Cleopatra extensively in *Jewish Antiquities* XIV–XV and *Against Apion*, particularly her dealings with Herod, Antony’s territorial grants, and Judean and Arabian revenues. His reports derive substantially from Herodian traditions and include hostile allegations—such as Cleopatra attempting to seduce or entrap Herod—which are not independently established. [Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities* XV](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/josephus/ant-15.html)

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Cleopatra met Caesar in Alexandria in late 48 BCE while he arbitrated the Ptolemaic succession. Their ensuing political and sexual relationship restored her to the throne after the Alexandrian War; she later lived at Caesar’s gardens in Rome in 46–44 BCE. Cleopatra publicly identified Caesar as the father of Caesarion, although the child’s biological paternity was disputed in Roman political discourse. Caesar’s placement of a gilded statue of Cleopatra in the Temple of Venus Genetrix further attests their public political association. [Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Lives/Caesar%2A.html), [Suetonius, *Divus Julius*](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Suetonius/12Caesars/Julius%2A.html)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact (later literary report):** In *Natural History* 9.119–121, completed about 77 CE, Pliny made Cleopatra the protagonist of the famous pearl-banquet story, claiming that she dissolved and drank an extraordinarily valuable pearl during a wager with Antony. Pliny unquestionably wrote the account, but the incident itself is an uncorroborated luxury exemplum composed roughly a century after the alleged event. [Pliny, *Natural History* IX](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0137%3Abook%3D9&force=y)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact (near-contemporary later historiography):** Strabo, writing after Cleopatra’s death and after visiting Roman Egypt, summarized her exile, restoration by Caesar, alliance with Antony, defeat, and suicide in *Geography* XVII. He preserves two alternative mechanisms for her death—an asp bite or poisonous ointment—making his account evidence for early uncertainty rather than proof of either method. No personal meeting between Strabo and Cleopatra is documented. [Strabo, *Geography* XVII.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Strabo/17A2%2A.html)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact (Augustan literary representation):** Virgil portrayed Cleopatra retrospectively in the Actium tableau on Aeneas’s shield in *Aeneid* VIII, written during the 20s BCE. He presents her as the unnamed Egyptian queen commanding foreign forces and gods against Augustus. This is documented Augustan victory poetry and political representation, not neutral testimony or evidence that Virgil personally encountered Cleopatra. [Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0054%3Abook%3D8)
Cleopatra later ruled Alexandria, the city founded by Alexander and associated with his tomb.
Solinus wrote about Cleopatra as the famous example associated with obtaining a deadly asp.
Paul wrote about Cleopatra’s relationships with Caesar and Mark Antony, her receipt of the Egyptian kingdom, and her eventual defeat.

- **[T1-]** In *On Animals* 9.61 Aelian discusses the tradition that Cleopatra VII (69–30 BCE) died through the bite of an asp, treating animal behaviour as evidence bearing on the reported manner of her death. **Documented fact** that Aelian wrote about Cleopatra; death by deliberately applied snakebite is a **reported fact/disputed historical tradition**, not something Aelian could have witnessed ([*On Animals* 9.61](https://topostext.org/work/560); [Attalus ancient-source index for Cleopatra](https://www.attalus.org/names/c/cleopatra.html)).

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Bradshaw’s fictional survey of world history in *The Goddess of Atvatabar* (1892) pairs Cleopatra with Antony during White’s account of Greece and Rome to Lyone. Nothing in the passage supports a connection beyond this authored reference. [Project Gutenberg text, chapter XXII](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/32825/32825-h/32825-h.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact.** Kerckhoffs’s doctoral dissertation, completed at Tübingen in 1876 and published at Paderborn in 1877, examined Daniel Casper von Lohenstein’s tragedies with particular attention to *Cleopatra*. The connection is literary-historical: he wrote about Lohenstein’s dramatic representation of Cleopatra, not from access to an ancient object or source associated directly with her. ([“Kerckhoffs’ Legacy”](https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/556))
Clovis was Clotilde’s husband and the father of her children.
Clotilde later interpreted or performed Debussy’s Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune.
Duncan and Clotilde belonged to the milieu of European modern dance, with Duncan’s free-dance example forming part of the context for Clotilde’s work.
A copy of Clotilde’s autobiography survives in the Mary Wigman family archive.
Rilke was a documented correspondent and admirer of Clotilde.
Clotilde developed her work within the Munich avant-garde milieu associated with Kandinsky, the Neue Künstlervereinigung, and the Blue Rider.
Bara belonged to Clotilde Sakharoff’s wider artistic network through her studies with Alexander Sacharoff and Moissey Kogan’s written comparison of them.
Clotilde was Clovis’s wife and queen, the mother of four of his known children, and Gregory of Tours’s principal advocate for his conversion.
Clovis was posthumously connected to the earlier Constantine through a literary model of battlefield victory, conversion, and Christian kingship.
The later Charlemagne inherited the Frankish-Christian royal tradition associated with Clovis and used a name for his son linguistically continuous with Clovis’s.
Clovis was posthumously associated with the earlier Jesus through baptismal-age symbolism and Christian sacred chronology.
Louis XIV was linked to the earlier Clovis through their related royal names and the Reims sacral-monarchy tradition.
The later Joan of Arc shared with Clovis a symbolic connection to Reims as a site of French sacred monarchy.
The Merovingian royal world associated with Clovis became linked posthumously to Denis through elite burials near the saint’s shrine and later dynastic patronage.
Chanel and Dior were competing figures in postwar Paris couture whose houses promoted opposing models of women’s dress.
Chanel and Balenciaga belonged to the same Paris couture milieu and were reportedly mutually respectful competitors.
Chanel housed Stravinsky and his family around 1920, supported his artistic work, and maintained a documented friendship with him.
Chanel financially supported Diaghilev and collaborated with his Ballets Russes by designing costumes, notably for Le Train Bleu.
Chanel and Picasso were friends in the Cocteau-Diaghilev circle and collaborated on Antigone and Le Train Bleu.
Chanel and Balanchine intersected professionally through a Ballets Russes production around 1929, although direct personal collaboration was not established.
Balenciaga and Chanel had a professional friendship in Paris couture, exchanged gifts, and later became estranged after a quarrel.
Chanel had a reported post-founder customer relationship with the Vuitton house, whose archives preserve lock information for her luggage.

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** They worked on two Cocteau theatrical productions: *Antigone* at the Théâtre de l’Atelier in 1922, for which Picasso supplied sets and masks and Chanel the costumes, and Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes production *Le Train Bleu* in 1924, for which Picasso supplied the front curtain and program while Chanel designed costumes. [Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza](https://www.museothyssen.org/en/exhibitions/picasso-chanel)
Columbus engaged with Aristotle's geographical proposition through medieval cosmographical texts.
Columbus encountered textual traditions connecting Aristotle's geographical knowledge with Alexander's conquests and information-gathering.
Columbus closely read and annotated Marco Polo's work, which shaped his ideas about Asia, its islands, wealth, and distances.
Columbus owned and annotated an Italian edition of Pliny's Natural History and drew geographical and natural-historical material from it.
Columbus encountered geographical propositions associated with Strabo through other works that he read.
Columbus received Bacon's argument for a limited westward ocean chiefly through Pierre d'Ailly and later cited Bacon as an authority.
Columbus used Augustinian theology, chronology, and historical frameworks in the Book of Prophecies.
Columbus engaged, often through compilers and commentaries, with theological material attributed to Aquinas in the compilation surrounding the Book of Prophecies.
Influenced by Polo's account, Columbus carried letters intended for an Asian sovereign whom he expected to encounter, associating his mission with Kublai Khan's court.
Piri's 1513 map identified a map by Columbus as a source and reported testimony attributed to a participant in Columbus's voyages.
Magellan's expedition later followed the westward transoceanic route toward Asian commerce that Columbus had sought to establish.
Cortés entered the Spanish Caribbean milieu in 1504 while Columbus was returning from Jamaica, although no personal meeting is established.
Pizarro later participated in the Caribbean and mainland expansion conducted through institutions and routes established after Columbus's voyages.

text: Inca Garcilaso later wrote about Columbus by circulating the unverified story that an unknown pilot had secretly informed him of western lands.
Humboldt later wrote an extensive historical study reconstructing Columbus's sources, calculations, and role in geographical knowledge.
Harari presents Columbus’s 1492 voyage as an example of European exploration of the unknown while situating it within imperial conquest.
Kennedy invoked Columbus through conventional presidential observances and Italian-American civic symbolism.
Bellamy later used Columbus’s 1492 voyage as the national-origin symbol for the National Public-School Celebration of its four-hundredth anniversary.
Guamán Poma incorporated Columbus into his universal and conquest history using material adapted from European sources.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact.** In the preface to *Sacred Mysteries* (1886), Le Plongeon discussed Columbus—under the Spanish form “Cristobal Colon”—and his 1498 sighting and navigation of the northern South American coast. [Primary text](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/57458/57458-h/57458-h.htm)
Roger Bacon's geographical calculations entered a textual tradition later available to proponents of westward travel associated with Christopher Columbus.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Wells narrated Columbus’s westward voyage and its place in European overseas expansion in *The Outline of History* and *A Short History of the World*. [Primary text](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/35461/35461-h/35461-h.htm)
Miranda invoked Columbus as a historical-symbolic figure by deriving the name Colombia from his name.
Cortés entered Hispaniola and its colonial system after Columbus’s voyages had helped establish it, without any documented meeting between them.
Brendan preceded Columbus in the Atlantic geographical tradition surrounding Brendan’s Island, which Columbus later knew.
Bartholdi modeled the earlier historical figure Columbus for a Tiffany display at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition.

- **[T1-]** **Reported fact:** Trincado wrote about Columbus’s identity and voyage, advancing the theory that Columbus came from Galicia—specifically the Pontevedra area—was probably Jewish, and possessed prior knowledge of Caribbean lands from an earlier storm-driven Atlantic crossing. Later authors explicitly attribute this argument to Trincado, but the accessible citations do not establish it as accepted history; the biographical and pre-discovery claims remain an **allegation or theory**. [Account attributing the argument to Trincado](https://www.kienyke.com/kien-fue/cristobal-colon-el-ladron-que-descubrio-america)
Leif and Columbus were posthumously linked through rival claims concerning the European discovery of America, with Leif presented as the earlier claimant.
Garvey used Columbus as a historical symbol while contesting European narratives of discovery.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Rodríguez discussed Columbus in his mature writings, calling him a virtuous Italian who did not intend slaughter but “opened the doors” to conquistadors whom he mistakenly trusted as Christians. This is direct written engagement with the earlier figure, preserved in Rodríguez’s *Obras completas*. [Text of Rodríguez’s works](https://biblioteca.clacso.edu.ar/clacso/se/20190926042843/Simon_Rodriguez_Obras_Completas.pdf)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Columbus appears repeatedly in *The Goddess of Atvatabar* (1892). White includes him in his historical account to Lyone; another character compares discovery of the interior world with Columbus’s discovery of America; and a fictional newspaper declares White’s renown greater than that of Columbus and Magellan. These are literary comparisons within the novel, not claims of personal or institutional linkage. [Project Gutenberg text, chapters XXII, XLIV, and LIX](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/32825/32825-h/32825-h.htm)
Clemens treated Columbus as a historical subject in his travel writing and satire of heroic national mythology.
Verne treated this earlier traveler as a subject within his histories of great voyages and the documentary source-world of the Voyages extraordinaires.

- **[T1-]** The *Legenda aurea* includes a dedicated life of Christopher, one of the principal medieval channels for the familiar story of the giant carrying the Christ child. **Documented fact** (textual connection); the narrative is **hagiographical legend**. [Fordham contents](https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/source/voragine1.asp)

- **[T1-]** Besant, the later figure, wrote and lectured about Saint-Germain as “Master Rákóczi,” placing him within a Theosophical hierarchy of Masters in the early twentieth century. She also reported that an apparition or adept appeared to her in 1898 and supplied the name “Rakoczi”; this is **documented religious testimony, not a documented meeting with the eighteenth-century man**. The development is summarized in the scholarly *Dictionary of Gnosis and Western Esotericism*. ([Brill reference entry](https://referenceworks.brill.com/display/entries/DGWO/DGWE-322.xml))

- **[T1+]** Waite, writing long after Saint-Germain’s death, examined the alleged Saint-Germain–Cagliostro relationship in his historical-occult studies. He judged the evidence for Cagliostro’s supposed initiation by Saint-Germain to be extremely weak. **Documented fact: later critical writing about Saint-Germain; no personal crossing.** ([“Saint-Germain and Cagliostro”](https://www.alchemy-texts.com/book/saint-germain-and-cagliostro/))

- **[T1-]** Blavatsky discussed Saint-Germain in *Isis Unveiled* (1877) and published “Count de Saint-Germain” in *The Theosophist* in May 1881, defending him as an occult adept and helping establish his posthumous Theosophical identity. **Documented fact: later written engagement; supernatural characterizations are religious claims.** ([Blavatsky’s 1881 article](https://neoterra-theosophy.com/biblio/blavatsky/hpb_cw/articles/v3/y1881_039.htm), [scholarly synthesis](https://referenceworks.brill.com/display/entries/DGWO/DGWE-322.xml))

- **[T5]** Later accounts claim that Cagliostro and his wife visited Saint-Germain in Holstein and received initiation, occult instruction, or an elixir from him, ostensibly before Saint-Germain’s death in 1784. The story entered print in sensational Cagliostro literature, including *Mémoires authentiques pour servir à l’histoire du comte de Cagliostro* (1785), but no secure letter, visitor record, or testimony from Prince Charles of Hesse establishes the meeting. **Rumor or myth: alleged personal meeting and discipleship, not documented fact.** ([Waite’s source-critical discussion](https://www.alchemy-texts.com/book/saint-germain-and-cagliostro/), [Brill reference entry](https://referenceworks.brill.com/display/entries/DGWO/DGWE-322.xml))

- **[T1-]** Steiner, the later figure, repeatedly wrote and lectured about Saint-Germain, notably in a lecture of 27 September 1911, identifying him through clairvoyant/reincarnation doctrine with Christian Rosenkreuz. **Documented fact: later written and oral discourse about Saint-Germain; the asserted identity is an Anthroposophical religious claim, not documentary biography.** ([Rudolf Steiner Archive](https://rsarchive.org/Lectures/GA130/English/RSP1984/19110927p01.html))
The Comte de Saint-Germain and Mesmer are associated through their later grouping in histories of Western esotericism rather than through documented personal contact.
Constantine the Great established Constantinople as his imperial capital, and Constantine XI later ruled and died defending the same Roman capital.
Justinian I commissioned the surviving principal structure of Hagia Sophia, which Constantine XI later used as the inherited imperial cathedral.
Constantine later sponsored churches at sites associated with Jesus’s birth, death, and resurrection.
Constantine’s regime was traditionally credited with sponsoring an early basilica at the Roman site venerated as Paul’s tomb.
Constantine later engaged with Alexander’s imperial image, including by placing an image of Alexander in Constantinople.
Constantine XI later ruled from Constantinople, the city founded by Constantine the Great.
Justinian later ruled from Constantine’s city and rebuilt major church sites originally associated with Constantine.
Otto III invoked Constantine as an earlier model of Christian Roman emperorship and addressed the Donation of Constantine in his diploma.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** In the recorded 2008 Project Camelot interview *Takeover of Planet Earth*, Maxwell presented Constantine as the ruler who codified Christianity in the fourth century and incorporated older religious material into it. The recording documents Maxwell’s theory; its historical formulation should not be treated as independently established by the interview. [Interview transcript](https://www.znakovi-vremena.net/en/Jordan_Maxwell-Takeover_of_Planet_Earth.pdf)
Theodora was buried in 548 in the Justinianic mausoleum at the Church of the Holy Apostles complex, where Constantine had earlier established his mausoleum and been interred.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Wells discussed Constantine’s conversion, imperial religious policy, and role in the political establishment of Christianity in *The Outline of History* and its shorter adaptation. [Primary text](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/35461/35461-h/35461-h.htm)

- **[T9+]** In the fourth century Constantine constructed the first monumental basilica around the Vatican memorial then revered as Peter’s tomb, physically enclosing the earlier “Trophy of Gaius.” Peter is the earlier/originating party in this site connection; Constantine is the later monumentalizer. Constantine’s building project and its orientation around the memorial are **documented facts**; identification of the underlying grave as Peter’s actual burial place is a **reported fact** grounded in ancient Roman Christian tradition, not a forensic certainty. [St. Peter’s Basilica, “The Tomb of Saint Peter”](https://www.basilicasanpietro.va/en/san-pietro/the-tomb-of-saint-peter)
Clovis was posthumously connected to the earlier Constantine through a literary model of battlefield victory, conversion, and Christian kingship.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** In a geographical-historical digression, Vigenère reported Chalkokondyles’ account that a Georgian queen’s healing by a Christian woman during Constantine’s reign led to her people’s conversion. This is documented as Vigenère’s retelling of a source, not independently verified history. [Primary-text transcription, fol. 316r](https://wulfric.artsci.utoronto.ca/rentexte/vigenere/chif_traite.htm)
Paul narrated Constantine’s accession, wars, rule, religious policies, and relationship with the Christian Church.
A Constantinian oration interpreted Virgil’s Eclogue 4 as a prophecy of Christ, though the oration’s precise authorship is disputed.
Pitois wrote about Constantine’s wars, consolidation of the Roman Empire, and political relationship with Christianity.
Reuchlin produced a Latin translation of a Greek biographical text about Constantine.
Later tradition connected Constantine with a church allegedly established at Eustace's former house or martyrdom site.
Acacius preceded Constantine's alleged foundation of a Constantinopolitan church dedicated to him and associated with his relics.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Augustine wrote about Constantine in *City of God* V.25–26, presenting his imperial success, Christian worship, donations, and clemency as evidence that temporal prosperity can be granted to a Christian ruler without constituting Christianity’s ultimate reward. Augustine was born seventeen years after Constantine’s death, so no personal crossing occurred.
Egeria worshipped in and described Jerusalem churches produced by Constantine’s imperial building program.

- **[T1-]** Jacobus wrote about Constantine principally within the *Legenda aurea* life of Pope Sylvester, transmitting medieval accounts of Constantine’s illness, conversion, baptism, and privileges granted to the Roman Church. **Documented fact** that Jacobus transmitted the narrative; important elements derive from the **legendary Sylvester tradition**, rather than contemporary fourth-century evidence. [Latin-text contents](https://www.hs-augsburg.de/homes/harsch/Chronologia/Lspost13/JacobusVoragine/jav_l000.html)
Vanderbilt met President Abraham Lincoln at the Executive Mansion on 17 March 1862 and offered his steamship for wartime use as a gift.
In 1872, Vanderbilt’s railroad interests entered written freight arrangements that benefited Rockefeller’s refining enterprise through a per-barrel rebate.
Mark Twain wrote about Vanderbilt in a satirical open letter published in March 1869.
Cortés personally met Motecuhzoma in Tenochtitlan, where Motecuhzoma subsequently became a captive under Spanish control.
The woman identified as Malintzin or Marina accompanied Cortés as his interpreter and diplomatic intermediary and was also his sexual partner and the mother of his son Martín.
Cortés and Pizarro were both in the orbit of Charles V’s court in the late 1520s, although no personal meeting was securely documented.
Cortés entered Hispaniola and its colonial system after Columbus’s voyages had helped establish it, without any documented meeting between them.

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Cortés wrote extensively about Motecuhzoma—his court, dominions, reception of the Spaniards, captivity, and death—in the *Second Letter to Charles V*, signed **30 October 1520**. The connection is certain, though the letter’s claims about voluntary submission and responsibility for Motecuhzoma’s death are partisan and contested. [Early Americas Digital Archive](https://eada.lib.umd.edu/text-entries/second-letter-of-hernando-cortes-to-charles-v/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Vigenère wrote that pictorial records were found at Mexico-Tenochtitlan when Cortés conquered it for Charles V, using the report to introduce nonalphabetic records in the *Traicté des chiffres*. The passage is documentary evidence of Vigenère’s written treatment, not of personal contact. [Primary-text transcription, fol. 11r](https://wulfric.artsci.utoronto.ca/rentexte/vigenere/chif_traite.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Trincado devoted a chapter of *La Revolución de México y el crimen de Norteamérica*, written in 1914, to Mexico through the age of Cortés. He acknowledged Cortés’s military ability and interpreted the Spanish victory over Moctezuma as an instrument of a metaphysical law driving the eventual unification of humanity. - **[T1-]** In *When Species Meet* (2007/08), Haraway directly engaged and criticized Guattari and Gilles Deleuze’s account of “becoming-animal,” arguing that their treatment of domestic animals and pet relations retained an anthropocentric preference for the wild, exceptional, or pack-like animal. This is a **documented fact** based on the book’s opening discussion and subsequent scholarly analysis of that critique ([book text](https://syllabus.pirate.care/_preview/library/Donna%20Haraway/When%20Species%20Meet%20%2839%29/When%20Species%20Meet%20-%20Donna%20Haraway.pdf); [Oxford review](https://academic.oup.com/isle/article-abstract/16/4/876/666951)).

- **[T1-]** Haraway wrote at length “with and against” Deleuze and Guattari’s “becoming-animal” in *When Species Meet*, contrasting it with her own “becoming-with” and defending historically situated relations involving actual domestic animals. This is a **documented fact**, not evidence that Haraway personally met either thinker ([Oxford review](https://academic.oup.com/isle/article-abstract/16/4/876/666951); [critical study](https://philpapers.org/rec/WILHCD-2)).

- **[T1-]** In *Staying with the Trouble* (2016), Haraway explicitly addressed Lovecraft while denying that her “Chthulucene” was named for his Cthulhu; she instead emphasized chthonic beings and the spider *Pimoa cthulhu*. She characterized Lovecraft’s monster and imaginative world in relation to misogyny and racial nightmare. This is a **documented fact**. The claim that Lovecraft directly inspired the concept is a **disputed theory**: Haraway denied a conscious derivation, although the spider’s scientific name itself was coined in reference to Lovecraft ([published critical discussion quoting Haraway](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/367185890_Into_the_sightless_vortex_of_the_unimaginable_Nyarlathotep_or_the_trajectory_of_the_Lovecraftian_signifier); [etymological critique](https://viewpointmag.com/2017/05/08/cthulhu-plays-no-role-for-me/)).

- **[T1-]** Haraway made Derrida’s writings on animals—particularly his encounter with a cat and his distinction between response and reaction—a sustained interlocutor in *When Species Meet* (2007/08). She praised his recognition that actual animals look back at humans but criticized his failure to become more curious about the particular cat and biological knowledge of cats. This is a **documented fact** ([University of Minnesota Press](https://www.upress.umn.edu/9780816650460/when-species-meet/); [book text](https://syllabus.pirate.care/_preview/library/Donna%20Haraway/When%20Species%20Meet%20%2839%29/When%20Species%20Meet%20-%20Donna%20Haraway.pdf)).

- **[T1-]** Haraway repeatedly engaged Marx’s categories of labor, production, capital, class, and technological transformation, most conspicuously in “‘Gender’ for a Marxist Dictionary” and “A Manifesto for Cyborgs” (1985). The latter deliberately reworked the manifesto form for socialist-feminist politics while criticizing Marxist traditions that inadequately explained gendered, racialized, reproductive, and informational labor. This is a **documented fact**, not a claim of doctrinal Marxism or personal connection ([original manifesto text](https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/donna-haraway-a-cyborg-manifesto); [Encyclopedia of Anthropology](https://ea.fflch.usp.br/en/node/61)).

- **[T3]** Haraway encountered Heidegger’s philosophy as a Colorado College student in the early-to-mid 1960s through Glenn Gray’s teaching and subsequently discussed that intellectual formation in autobiographical interviews. This is a **reported fact** grounded in Haraway’s retrospective testimony; no personal meeting or correspondence with Heidegger is documented.

- **[T1-]** Haraway directly engaged Foucault’s accounts of biopolitics, clinical knowledge, discipline, sexuality, and modern power. In the 1985 cyborg manifesto she called Foucauldian biopolitics a limited premonition of cyborg politics and cited *The Birth of the Clinic*, *The History of Sexuality*, and *Discipline and Punish* while arguing that late-twentieth-century technoscience required a further analytic step. This is a **documented fact**; no personal meeting or correspondence is established ([manifesto text](https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/donna-haraway-a-cyborg-manifesto)).

- **[T1-]** Haraway engaged the cybernetic field established by Wiener—communication and control across animals and machines, feedback, information, automation, and military power—in the work culminating in “A Manifesto for Cyborgs” (1985). The connection is a **documented intellectual genealogy**, mediated partly through G. Evelyn Hutchinson’s systems-ecology milieu. No teacher–student relationship, correspondence, collaboration, or meeting between Wiener and Haraway is documented.

counterpart_name: Simone Lucie Ernestine Marie Bertrand de Beauvoir
text: - **[T1-]** In “‘Gender’ for a Marxist Dictionary,” Haraway traced modern feminist meanings of gender to Beauvoir’s proposition that one is not born but becomes a woman, while situating that proposition within later socialist-feminist debates over sex, labor, and historical construction. This is a **documented fact**; no personal meeting between Haraway and Beauvoir was established ([discussion of Haraway’s formulation](https://cadmus.eui.eu/bitstreams/ceef047f-d2dd-51e3-9e7e-429ef8952b4a/download)).

- **[T3]** Haraway reports reading Aquinas from about age thirteen during her Catholic education in Denver and has discussed Thomism, sacramental realism, incarnation, and the materiality of signs as formative—even after her departure from Catholic belief. This is a **reported fact** from autobiographical testimony and filmed interviews, not evidence of continuing Thomist orthodoxy ([documentary record](https://www.docuseek2.com/if-donna); [*How Like a Leaf*](https://attachments.are.na/632919/706257a5039d513c87d42c531c69c4de.pdf?1465734125=)).
Hoyer danced in Wigman’s Tanzgesänge ensemble, and Wigman later supported Hoyer’s American Dance Festival invitation and cast her in Le Sacre du printemps.
Hoyer wrote two published texts about the earlier-born Wigman in 1951 and 1956.
Hoyer worked with leading American dancers including Graham and studied Graham’s methods during the 1957 American Dance Festival.
Hoyer’s 1957 article about American modern dance and New York studios was catalogued as engaging with the earlier-born Graham.
Hoyer worked with Humphrey and encountered her methods during the 1957 American Dance Festival.
Hoyer made direct professional contact with Limón and learned his methods during the 1957 American Dance Festival.
Hoyer’s 1957 article about American modern dance and New York studios was catalogued as engaging with the earlier-born Holm.
Hoyer trained in the Trümpy school environment associated with Skoronel, although direct teacher-pupil contact is uncertain.
Hoyer belonged to Wigman’s third group and participated in the artistic milieu connected with the 1936 Olympic production.
Humphrey met and studied under Ruth St. Denis at Denishawn, joined her company, co-choreographed works with her, and later corresponded with her amid their deteriorating relationship.
Humphrey met Ted Shawn at Denishawn and worked under him in several roles before artistic and managerial disputes led to their break in 1928.
Humphrey and Martha Graham were Denishawn contemporaries who later jointly founded the Dance Repertory Theatre and worked within the same institutional networks.
Humphrey and Hanya Holm shared the founding artistic milieu of the Bennington School of the Dance in the summer of 1934.
José Limón became Humphrey’s student and dancer, later co-founded the Limón Dance Company with her, and worked closely with her as its artistic director and choreographer.
Humphrey engaged posthumously with Federico García Lorca’s writing by basing her 1946 work Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías on his elegy.
Humphrey later used and valued Rudolf Laban’s movement-notation system, through which numerous examples of her choreography were preserved.
Archival collections document correspondence between St. Denis and Humphrey in both directions.
Cunningham encountered Humphrey through the late-1930s Mills and Bennington summer dance programs in California.
Muller adopted Humphrey's fall-and-rebound principle through the pedagogical lineage transmitted by José Limón.
Hoyer worked with Humphrey and encountered her methods during the 1957 American Dance Festival.
Humphrey and Graham were Denishawn contemporaries who later participated in the same Bennington modern-dance milieu.
Poe and Dickens met in Philadelphia in March 1842 and discussed literature, American poetry, and Poe’s efforts to secure British publication.
Poe read and discussed Bulwer-Lytton’s writing, whose fictional Francis Vivian also influenced Griswold’s posthumous portrayal of Poe.
Poe wrote within Gothic and speculative traditions previously transformed by Mary Shelley.
Verne explicitly continued and attempted to explain Poe’s The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym in Le Sphinx des glaces.
Doyle identified Poe as a founder of detective fiction and Dupin as a precursor to Sherlock Holmes.
Lovecraft repeatedly discussed Poe, wrote “The Poe-et’s Nightmare,” and presented him as a central predecessor in Supernatural Horror in Literature.
Borges read, discussed, translated, and anthologized Poe as part of the detective and fantastic traditions transmitted in Spanish.
Bioy Casares helped include Poe within the detective and fantastic traditions transmitted in Spanish.
Debussy developed unfinished operatic adaptations of Poe’s works, especially La chute de la maison Usher and Le diable dans le beffroi.
King repeatedly placed Poe within the ancestry of modern horror.
Poe engaged in writing with contemporary scientific and exploratory debates associated here with Darwin, although no personal exchange is documented.
Poe’s Philadelphia residence and cipher writing connected him to an American intellectual tradition previously represented there by Franklin.
Later accounts report that Lincoln read or admired Poe, particularly “The Raven,” though the claim lacks support from a contemporary Lincoln document.
Sonrel engaged with Poe's work by basing her 1904 Salon painting Ligéia on his story “Ligeia.”
Elizebeth Smith Friedman and William F. Friedman discussed Edgar Allan Poe’s acrostics in The Shakespearean Ciphers Examined.
Benjamin analyzed Poe's crowd stories and their relationship to Baudelaire, the flâneur, and modern urban perception.
Artaud read Poe during adolescence and received a literary influence from his work.
Jabotinsky engaged with Poe's writing by translating “The Raven” and “Annabel Lee” into Hebrew.
Lacan analyzed Poe's “The Purloined Letter” as a model for the circulation of the signifier.
Cirlot wrote about Poe, whose work also influenced his literary symbolism.
Poe and Hugo were connected only through the broader French Romantic literary environment in which Poe’s work was subsequently received.
Veroni later issued editions of Poe’s Dos poemas and Annabel Lee as a posthumous editorial and artistic engagement with Poe’s writings.
Jarry engaged textually with Poe by acknowledging his influence and including his work among Dr Faustroll’s livres pairs.
Friedman assessed Poe's cryptographic interests and accomplishments in his 1936 article “Edgar Allan Poe, Cryptographer.”
As a teenager, Culianu engaged one-sidedly with Poe’s writings by translating them into Romanian.
Halley met Newton, encouraged and financed publication of the Principia, mediated his dispute with Hooke, and later collaborated with him in scientific and official affairs.
Halley and Hooke were Royal Society colleagues who discussed planetary dynamics together, and Halley conveyed Hooke's gravitational priority claim to Newton.
Biographical literature reports personal contact between Halley and Huygens within the continental scientific network.
Halley and Leibniz occupied overlapping Royal Society and continental mathematical correspondence networks, although no close friendship is established.
Halley cited Kepler's observations and used his planetary laws when discussing orbital motion and comparing the comets of 1607 and 1682.
Laplace wrote about Halley’s astronomical work and his role in encouraging Newton to publish the propositions that became the Principia.
Hooke corresponded directly with Halley about comet observations and other notices, while Halley later conveyed messages between Hooke and Newton.
Rostand wrote La Princesse lointaine, a theatrical treatment of Rudel’s legend.
Lagrange later recalled and evaluated a paper by Halley as the work that awakened his interest in mathematics.
Elsztain met Soros in New York City in 1990 and formed a substantial investment partnership focused on Argentine real estate.
Fernández de Kirchner received Elsztain for a private meeting at Argentina's Casa Rosada in May 2008.
Elsztain joined a Jewish organizational delegation that met Chávez at Miraflores Palace in Caracas in August 2008.
Elsztain and Netanyahu attended the World Jewish Congress's 13th Plenary Assembly in Jerusalem in January 2009, without a documented private interaction.
Elsztain and Milei had repeated personal meetings and traveled together during 2023–25, including a joint visit to Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson's grave.
Edward Bellamy and his cousin Francis Julius Bellamy were personally related and participated in connected Christian-socialist and Nationalist currents.
William Morris reviewed and criticized Bellamy’s Looking Backward, offered News from Nowhere as a socialist counter-utopia, and Bellamy later issued a response using the same title.
Frank Lloyd Wright engaged Bellamy’s writings posthumously as an influence on his ideas about decentralized democratic planning.
John Dewey wrote about the earlier Bellamy in his 1934 essay A Great American Prophet and promoted the revival of Bellamy’s work.
Erich Fromm interpreted the earlier Bellamy in his foreword to a 1960 edition of Looking Backward.
Theosophical literature reports that Blavatsky referred to or showed interest in Bellamy’s social-reform vision.
Bellamy wrote about the earlier Lincoln in his 1891 New Nation piece Lincoln’s Prophecy.
Francis Julius Bellamy was Edward Bellamy’s first cousin and engaged intellectually with the Christian-socialist and Nationalist milieu shaped partly by Edward’s novel Looking Backward.
Bellamy’s Looking Backward formed part of Rocker’s early socialist reading and intellectual development.
Bernays and Freud corresponded about family affairs, the American publication and promotion of Freud’s writings, royalties, and Bernays’s books.
Bernays visited his uncle Freud in Vienna and later assisted Freud’s family financially and editorially.
Bernays later wrote and spoke extensively about Freud and interpreted Freud’s ideas in relation to public relations.
As publicity manager for the Ballets Russes’ American engagement, Bernays created promotional materials concerning Diaghilev and his company.
Bernays promoted Nijinsky in writing before and during the Ballets Russes’ American seasons and later described him and the campaign.
Bernays directly engaged Edison as the principal living participant in the 1929 Light’s Golden Jubilee publicity campaign.
Bernays later wrote and spoke about Edison and the Light’s Golden Jubilee as a case study in constructing a national symbolic figure.
Curie and Bernays shared the milieu of the Light’s Golden Jubilee gathering in Dearborn on 21 October 1929.
Rossetti met Burne-Jones in 1856, became his informal teacher, collaborated with him, entered business with him, and corresponded with him.
Morris was Burne-Jones’s lifelong friend, housemate, collaborator, and business partner from their meeting at Oxford in 1853 until Morris’s death.
Burne-Jones knew Jane Morris through the Oxford and Pre-Raphaelite circle, and their families belonged to the same extended social network.
May Morris was known to the Burne-Jones family from childhood and later documented aspects of the shared Morris–Burne-Jones circle.
Christina Rossetti and Burne-Jones had social and artistic-circle contact within the wider Pre-Raphaelite milieu.
Ruskin met Burne-Jones in 1856 and became his mentor, patron, travel sponsor, and critic.
Burne-Jones and Millais belonged to the broader British Pre-Raphaelite institutional milieu, although no sustained personal collaboration was established.
Burne-Jones knew Hunt through the Rossetti and Morris circle and also corresponded with him.
Burne-Jones was socially associated with Wilde and reportedly provided financial assistance during Wilde’s legal crisis.
Yeats admired Burne-Jones and engaged with the dreamlike and symbolic aesthetics associated with his artistic legacy.
Burne-Jones admired and artistically engaged with Blake’s visionary work despite having no possibility of personal contact.
Modern scholarship describes Bernhardt as Burne-Jones’s friend, although their precise meetings and correspondence were not reconstructed.
Burne-Jones depicted Vivien as a major subject of Victorian Arthurian art, notably in The Beguiling of Merlin.
Burne-Jones belonged to an artistic milieu that represented Arthurian subjects including traditions concerning Lancelot, Guinevere, and Elaine.
Elizabeth engraved Burne-Jones’s Cupid and Psyche illustration and was trained to interpret his designs in embroidery.
Kelley personally collaborated and traveled with Dee for several years before their partnership dissolved amid disputes and rivalry.
Yates later wrote about Kelley within her influential historical interpretation of Renaissance angelic magic, alchemy, and Rosicrucian currents.
Waite later translated, compiled, and republished Kelley's alchemical writings and wrote a biographical preface about him.
Witten later worked at the Institute for Advanced Study, where Einstein had worked decades earlier, without their occupancies overlapping.
Witten used Feynman’s path-integral formalism in his later work, while no personal encounter between them is established.
Witten later developed baryon physics using Skyrme’s model and helped explain its topological character.
Witten joined the Institute for Advanced Study after Oppenheimer’s earlier tenure there as director, with no personal connection documented.
Dirac’s operators, monopoles, spinors, and constrained gauge systems became central objects in Witten’s later generation of mathematical physics.
Archival references in the Feynman Papers support professional correspondence between Feynman and Witten.
Witten’s 1983–84 large-N QCD work revisited and reinterpreted Skyrme’s earlier baryon model.
Egeria visited Carrhae/Harran and nearby sites identified by local Christians with Abraham and his family.
Egeria followed sacred sites and travel stations associated with Moses and the Exodus, including Sinai, the burning bush and Nebo.
Egeria worshipped at and described sites associated with Jesus’s life, death, resurrection and ascension.
Egeria traveled through Tarsus and other geographical settings associated with Paul.
Egeria deliberately visited Thecla’s shrine near Seleucia, whose cult influenced her itinerary.
Egeria worshipped in and described Jerusalem churches produced by Constantine’s imperial building program.
Justinian’s government later monumentalized the Sinai pilgrimage site whose earlier sanctuary and monastic complex Egeria had visited.

- **[T1+]** Egeria wrote about “holy Thecla” and her sanctuary in *Itinerarium* 22–23 after visiting Seleucia in Isauria, approximately AD 381–384. She records praying there, receiving communion, meeting the deaconess Marthana, and having the saint’s acts read. **Documented fact:** Egeria’s surviving travel narrative is eyewitness evidence for the late-fourth-century cult and institution, not for Thecla’s alleged first-century biography. [Egeria’s itinerary and shrine visit](https://portal.sds.ox.ac.uk/articles/online_resource/E05227_The_pilgrim_Egeria_in_her_Itinerary_writes_of_the_sanctuary_of_Thekla_follower_of_the_Apostle_Paul_S00092_in_Seleucia_ad_Calycadnum_Isauria_southern_Asia_Minor_where_she_prayed_and_read_a_passage_from_the_Acts_of_Thecla_Written_in_La/13867643)
Einstein publicly supported Noether’s mathematical work and academic standing amid debates about conservation laws in general relativity.
Einstein met Weizmann in 1921 and subsequently worked and corresponded with him on Zionist fundraising and Hebrew University affairs.
Einstein met Ben-Gurion at Princeton in 1951, before Ben-Gurion initiated the unsuccessful offer of Israel’s presidency to him.
Einstein corresponded and exchanged scientific arguments with Schrödinger about wave mechanics, entanglement, and the completeness of quantum theory.
Einstein and Fermi occupied the same international theoretical-physics milieu and attended major scientific gatherings, although no close collaboration is established.
Einstein and Oppenheimer shared the Institute for Advanced Study environment at Princeton, where Einstein supported and advised Oppenheimer during his security controversy.
Einstein met Curie through Solvay and European scientific circles and supported her during the hostile 1911 press campaign.
Einstein corresponded with Gandhi and expressed admiration for his nonviolent resistance and moral authority, though they never met.
Einstein met Bohr in 1920 and developed a close personal and intellectual relationship shaped by their continuing disagreements over quantum mechanics.
Einstein sent Tesla a formal seventy-fifth-birthday message in 1931, but the record does not support a broader friendship.
Einstein encountered Dirac through the international quantum-physics community and Solvay-era scientific gatherings.
Einstein met Tagore repeatedly in Germany in 1930 for published conversations about reality, truth, beauty, music, and the mind.
Bose sent Einstein his 1924 paper, which Einstein translated, arranged to publish, and extended into what became Bose–Einstein statistics.
Einstein chose Freud for a written League of Nations exchange about war that was published in 1933 as Warum Krieg?
Einstein and Heisenberg were scientific interlocutors and opponents within the Solvay debates over quantum mechanics.
Pauli corresponded with Einstein as a colleague and sometimes severe critic of Einstein’s unified-field research.
Einstein repeatedly wrote about and reformulated the mechanics and theory of gravitation associated with the earlier figure Newton.
Einstein explicitly discussed and reformulated the earlier Galilean concepts of relativity and inertia.
Einstein engaged with the earlier Maxwellian theory of electrodynamics as a central foundation of special relativity.
Einstein and Bergson confronted one another publicly in Paris in 1922 over the meaning of time.
Einstein’s relativity work followed and paralleled Poincaré’s earlier work on electrodynamics and synchronization, although direct dependence remains disputed.
Poincaré personally met and conversed with Einstein at the first Solvay Conference in 1911.
After the Solvay meeting, Poincaré wrote an assessment supporting Einstein’s candidacy for a chair at ETH Zürich.
Einstein visited Jung’s Zurich home several times before the First World War and discussed relativity with him.
Wiener met Einstein in the United States and later spent about five and a half hours traveling and conversing with him between Basel and Geneva.
Buber and Einstein corresponded and participated in overlapping Hebrew University and Jewish public-affairs networks.

- **[T4]** **Documented fact:** Einstein and Wells were present together at Wells’s 15 April 1929 address, “The Common Sense of World Peace,” in the Reichstag building in Berlin. A contemporary photograph places both men with German officials at the event. This securely establishes shared time and place; the available record does not justify enlarging it into a close scientific collaboration. [Contemporary report of the Reichstag address](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2021/apr/16/danger-of-drifting-into-war-hg-wells-addresses-reichstag-1929) [Photographic record](https://www.granger.com/results.asp?image=0196457)
Reich met Einstein in 1941 and subsequently disputed Einstein's conventional explanation of results from testing an orgone accumulator.
Max and Einstein corresponded in 1930 about a proposed agricultural-colonization project for Eastern European Jews in Peru.
Bose corresponded and collaborated scientifically with Einstein and met him in Berlin in 1925.
Turing wrote a youthful précis of Einstein’s theory of relativity.
Le Corbusier visited Einstein in Princeton in 1946, discussed the Modulor with him, and was photographed with him.
Franklin was a posthumous predecessor and cultural model for this later scientist working in a field transformed by electrical science.
Einstein publicly commended Rocker’s work and contributed a tribute for Rocker’s eightieth-birthday celebration.
Klein and Einstein corresponded substantively in 1918 about general relativity, conservation laws, and mathematical physics.
Einstein participated remotely in the international 1929 Golden Jubilee of Light commemoration honoring Edison.
Von Neumann attended Einstein’s Berlin lectures before they became colleagues at the Institute for Advanced Study.
Fermi met Einstein in international physics circles and later shared the American émigré nuclear-physics milieu with him.
Einstein reportedly attended Feynman’s Princeton seminar on absorber theory and asked a question about gravitation.

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Einstein joined Philip Murray, William Green, and other prominent Americans in a telegram dated 29 January 1943 urging Soviet authorities to release Erlich and Wiktor Alter. Because Erlich had secretly died in NKVD custody on 15 May 1942, the appeal was necessarily one-sided and made without knowledge of his death. A later U.S. government file records the telegram. [FBI file concerning Einstein and the Erlich–Alter case](https://www.theblackvault.com/documents/fbifiles/einstein3.pdf)
Gauss preceded Einstein in the mathematical tradition of intrinsic curved geometry that later underpinned general relativity.

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Ben-Gurion and Einstein exchanged views concerning Zionism, Israel, Jewish life, and public responsibility. After Chaim Weizmann’s death, Ben-Gurion directed Ambassador Abba Eban to ask Einstein in writing whether he would accept Israel’s presidency; Einstein declined on 18 November 1952. The formal offer therefore passed through Eban rather than being made during a personal encounter.
- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Einstein hosted Ben-Gurion at his Princeton home in May 1951; contemporary and later accounts identify this as a personal meeting, not merely simultaneous presence at Princeton. [The Atlantic](https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/2026/04/hasan-piker-einstein-democrats/686855/)
Einstein gave telephone assent to the 1948 public appeal organized by Fromm and appeared as one of its signatories.
Curie and Einstein corresponded from 1911 to 1932 and attended the 1911 and 1927 Solvay physics conferences together.
Witten later worked at the Institute for Advanced Study, where Einstein had worked decades earlier, without their occupancies overlapping.
Einstein wrote about Kepler’s scientific method and discoveries in a 1930 article and a later introduction to a book on Kepler.
Keyserling publicly defended Einstein in 1933 and praised his importance while rejecting nationalist claims that his Jewish identity made him non-German.
Glücksmann served on and financially supported the Buenos Aires committee that invited Einstein to Argentina.
Einstein was reported to be Landauer’s cousin, although the exact degree of kinship was not specified.

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** Bergson’s *Durée et simultanéité* (1922) was a sustained written engagement with Einstein’s relativity theory. It accepted the theory’s physical importance while disputing philosophical interpretations that Bergson believed reduced time entirely to clock measurements and coordinate systems. [Digitized edition](https://archive.org/details/dureetsimulta00berg)
- **[T4]** **Documented fact.** Bergson and Einstein were founding members of the League of Nations’ International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation and attended its inaugural Geneva session on 1 August 1922; Bergson chaired the committee. [United Nations–associated centenary record](https://intellectualcooperation.org/files/IntellectualCooperation_2022.pdf)

- **[T4]** **Documented fact.** Bergson and Einstein were founding members of the League of Nations’ International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation and attended its inaugural Geneva session on 1 August 1922; Bergson chaired the committee. [United Nations–associated centenary record](https://intellectualcooperation.org/files/IntellectualCooperation_2022.pdf)
Fuller reported meeting Einstein in New York around 1936 after Einstein read the manuscript of Nine Chains to the Moon.
Dewey and Einstein participated through correspondence and joint appeals in an international network addressing academic freedom, war, peace, and democratic rights.

- **[T5]** **Reported fact:** Recent chronological reconstruction concludes that Noether had returned to Göttingen before Einstein’s Wolfskehl lectures there in **June–July 1915** and therefore met him during his visit. No direct account of their conversation survives, so the meeting is strongly reconstructed rather than independently recorded in a diary or letter ([Rowe, 2024](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/andp.202300479)).
- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** After Noether’s death, Einstein wrote about her in a memorial letter published by the *New York Times* on **4 May 1935**, emphasizing her creative importance to modern algebra. Under the atlas convention, Noether receives the plus sign as the earlier, written-about figure ([Einstein memorial text](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Obituaries/Noether_Emmy_Einstein/)).

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** After Noether’s death, Einstein wrote about her in a memorial letter published by the *New York Times* on **4 May 1935**, emphasizing her creative importance to modern algebra. Under the atlas convention, Noether receives the plus sign as the earlier, written-about figure ([Einstein memorial text](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Obituaries/Noether_Emmy_Einstein/)).
Darwin and Einstein were later linked institutionally through their separate receipt of the Royal Society’s Copley Medal.
Einstein reportedly attended the 1934 New York premiere of a sympathetic film based on a fictionalized version of Joseph Süß Oppenheimer’s life.
Culianu wrote about Einstein’s relativistic universe when comparing traditional otherworld narratives with modern concepts of space, time, and additional dimensions.
Oppenheimer and Einstein met and conversed at Princeton about physics, government, and Oppenheimer’s security troubles.
Einstein made a one-sided written intervention concerning the imprisoned Alter by joining a telegram seeking his release and later disputing his alleged guilt in writing.

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Horkheimer met Einstein in the United States by February 1935. In a letter dated **20 February 1935**, Horkheimer thanked Einstein for their conversation and sent him the latest *Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung* and an English prospectus of the Institute.
- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** The same 1935 letter engaged Einstein on causality in the social sciences and requested his goodwill toward the Institute, establishing one-sided written intellectual engagement following their meeting. The letter is published in Horkheimer’s selected correspondence and reproduced in a [document collection concerning his sociology-of-knowledge fragments](https://jamescrane.substack.com/p/collectionhorkheimers-fragments-on).

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** The same 1935 letter engaged Einstein on causality in the social sciences and requested his goodwill toward the Institute, establishing one-sided written intellectual engagement following their meeting. The letter is published in Horkheimer’s selected correspondence and reproduced in a [document collection concerning his sociology-of-knowledge fragments](https://jamescrane.substack.com/p/collectionhorkheimers-fragments-on).
Einstein wrote to Mussolini in 1931 about academic freedom and the Fascist loyalty oath, and Mussolini’s office replied.
Garcilaso portrayed his maternal relative Atahualpa as a usurper and destroyer of Huáscar’s family in his historical reconstruction.
Garcilaso acknowledged, extensively used, and preserved fragments of Valera’s historical writing.
Garcilaso made Pizarro a central figure in his Historia general del Perú.
Garcilaso and Góngora were indirectly connected through documented inheritance and financial dealings in Córdoba.
Garcilaso’s Comentarios reales was associated with the intellectual environment of Condorcanqui’s rebellion, although Condorcanqui’s personal use of it remains uncertain.
Humboldt read and cited Garcilaso while interpreting Andean geography, monuments, and history.
San Martín’s government promoted the republication and circulation of Garcilaso’s work during the independence period.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact.** Le Plongeon cited Garcilaso de la Vega as an authority on ancient Peru in *Sacred Mysteries* (1886), incorporating his account into a comparison of American and Old World religious traditions. [Primary text](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/57458/57458-h/57458-h.htm)
Inca Garcilaso later wrote about Columbus by circulating the unverified story that an unknown pilot had secretly informed him of western lands.
Condorcanqui reportedly possessed Garcilaso’s Comentarios reales, although the work’s direct influence on rebel decisions is disputed.
Spence used and praised Garcilaso's Royal Commentaries of the Incas as a principal source on the Inca past.
Sonrel engaged with Poe's work by basing her 1904 Salon painting Ligéia on his story “Ligeia.”
Later catalogues report that Sonrel drew artistic inspiration from Dante's Vita nuova and Divina Commedia.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Swedenborg made Abraham a recurring subject of *Arcana Coelestia* (1749–56), his verse-by-verse spiritual interpretation of Genesis and Exodus. He treated the patriarchal narrative correspondentially rather than merely as biography. [Swedenborg Foundation](https://swedenborg.com/emanuel-swedenborg/writings/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Swedenborg read and excerpted Aristotle while developing his philosophical and psychological vocabulary; Aristotle appears among the historical authorities engaged in Swedenborg’s scientific notebooks and pre-theological works. This was textual engagement, not evidence of unmediated intellectual descent. [Scholarly overview of Swedenborg’s philosophical context](https://swedenborg-philosophy.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/10/Williams-Hogan_Article-New_Philosophy_January-June_2013.pdf)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Balzac studied Swedenborgian teaching and made Swedenborg and his doctrines explicit subjects in novels including *Louis Lambert* (1832) and *Séraphîta* (1835). The precise channels and extent of doctrinal dependence remain subjects of scholarship, but the written engagement itself is unmistakable. [Scholarly survey](https://swedenborg.com/scholars-swedenborgs-influence-on-balzac-and-strindberg/), [Persée study](https://www.persee.fr/doc/caief_0571-5865_1963_num_15_1_2263)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Borges repeatedly wrote and lectured about Swedenborg. His works include “Los ángeles de Swedenborg” in *El libro de los seres imaginarios* (1967), an essay used to open *Testimony to the Invisible*, and a lecture delivered at the University of Belgrano in Buenos Aires on 16 June 1978. [Bibliographic discussion](https://www.cervantesvirtual.com/s3/BVMC_OBRAS/ffb/d32/648/2b1/11d/fac/c70/021/85c/e60/64/mimes/ffbd3264-82b1-11df-acc7-002185ce6064_37.html), [book record](https://books.google.com/books/about/Testimony_to_the_Invisible.html?hl=en&id=rm9wNAAACAAJ&output=html_text)

[Swedenborg Foundation](https://swedenborg.com/emanuel-swedenborg/influence/), [discussion of the textual evidence](https://swedenborg.com/swedenborg-blake-the-everlasting-gospel/)

This was Doyle’s retrospective interpretation, not evidence that Swedenborg belonged to the nineteenth-century Spiritualist movement. [Cambridge University Press contents](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/history-of-spiritualism/frontmatter/27B697363574428952AABE8EEA86A512), [1926 text](https://www.arthur-conan-doyle.com/images/4/4d/The-history-of-spiritualism-vol1-cassell-1926.pdf)

[*Scribe of Heaven*, reception chapter](https://swedenborg.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/NCE_ScribeofHeaven.pdf)

Works such as *Doctrine of the Lord* (1763) and *True Christian Religion* (1771) argue that the divine and human are united in Jesus and reject a Trinity of three divine persons. [Swedenborg Foundation writings guide](https://swedenborg.com/emanuel-swedenborg/writings/)

Claims that Jung’s mature psychology was simply derived from Swedenborg go beyond this evidence. [Jung, *Memories, Dreams, Reflections* text](https://ratical.org/co-globalize/MemoriesDreamsReflections-Jung.pdf), [Swedenborg Society reception summary](https://www.swedenborg.org.uk/events/swedenborg-and-the-english-romantics-items-from-the-swedenborg-collection/)

The surviving film begins with an on-camera dialogue between the songwriter and singer before Gardel performs Discépolo’s tango, providing direct audiovisual evidence of their engagement. Fromm interpreted Abraham in his writings as a paradigmatic biblical hero whose departure from country and clan marks a movement from possession toward freedom.

Fromm examined and contrasted Jung's archetypal theory of dreams and myths with Freudian and historical-humanistic interpretations.
