- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Wells wrote retrospectively about Verne while distinguishing Verne’s extrapolative adventure machinery from his own “fantasies of possibility.” The comparison became central to later accounts of the origins of science fiction, but no well-supported personal meeting between Wells and Verne has been established.
Hugo and Verne are linked by documented correspondence and Verne’s stated admiration, while a personal meeting remains uncertain.
Verne served on the committee promoting and financing the Alexandre Dumas monument whose pedestal Bouvard and Gravigny designed.
Roca corresponded with Sarmiento from at least 1875, defending his military reputation before Sarmiento later criticized the Roca family's patronage.
Hernández participated in the Buenos Aires political coalition supporting Roca's candidacy during the struggles of approximately 1879–1880.
Roca appointed Alvear to administer Buenos Aires as the federal capital's first intendente under the reorganized municipal system.
Tamburini worked as an Argentine state architect in Buenos Aires during Roca's first presidency.
Ceferino was born at Chimpay in 1886, and Roca later visited the same site for a railway inauguration in 1899, although no meeting was established.
Della Valle's 1892 painting represented frontier conflict associated with the post-Conquest historical period shaped by Roca's campaigns.
Milei posthumously invoked Roca as a leading Argentine president and quoted his 1880 inaugural formulation in 2023.
Pedro Lagleyze facilitated contact between Della Valle and Roca, whom Della Valle then painted.
Roca and Buschiazzo were connected by their presence at the 1904 cornerstone ceremony for the Buschiazzo-designed Asilo Humberto Primo.
Roca commissioned the dossier’s subject to redesign the grounds of Estancia La Paz, establishing a direct patron–designer relationship.
Arslan was personally acquainted with Roca, who invited him to La Larga, encouraged his novel, and received its dedication.
Ceferino belonged to the post-conquest historical milieu created by Roca's campaign against Manuel Namuncurá's people, although no personal contact is documented.
Torcuato supported the coalition that brought Roca to power, received his municipal appointment from Roca, and was reportedly with him during an attack.
Py filmed President Roca at official events in Buenos Aires and Puerto Belgrano between 1900 and 1904.
Sarmiento interacted politically with Roca during the 1870s, supporting some measures while criticizing aspects of his political organization.
Bioy Casares moved in Cortázar’s Buenos Aires literary milieu and dedicated a copy of Crónicas de Bustos Domecq to him.
Cortázar engaged in writing with Camus’s existential thought, although no personal meeting or correspondence is established.
Cortázar engaged with Breton’s surrealist ideas as formative influences on his treatment of chance, poetic reality, and the marvelous.
Cortázar and Piazzolla belonged to the same transatlantic cultural milieu as prominent Argentine expatriate artists in Paris.
Cortázar publicly opposed and denounced Pinochet’s dictatorship through political advocacy and related writings.
Cortázar invoked Gardel and tango in his written remembrance of Buenos Aires.
Cortázar wrote about Guevara after his death and helped memorialize him as a revolutionary figure.
Cortázar addressed correspondence and public appeals to Castro while maintaining a critically supportive relationship with the Cuban Revolution.
García Márquez was Cortázar’s friend, correspondent, political interlocutor, and travel companion.
Cortázar traveled with Fuentes and García Márquez in Czechoslovakia in 1968.
Cortázar and Sartre participated in the same written political intervention by signing the 1971 letter to Fidel Castro about the Padilla affair.
Borges published Cortázar’s Casa tomada, while Cortázar acknowledged Borges’s literary influence before their later political divergence.
Cortázar opposed Perón and Peronism politically and later reassessed the movement’s popular base.
Cortázar engaged with Klee’s art within his broader interest in modern visual art and collage aesthetics.
Cortázar was in Chile around Allende’s 1970 inauguration and supported Allende’s Popular Unity government.

counterpart_name: Simone Lucie Ernestine Marie Bertrand de Beauvoir
text: Beauvoir and Cortázar jointly signed the first intellectuals’ letter to Fidel Castro concerning the Padilla affair.
Ocampo’s Sur served as a shared literary institution in which Cortázar later published criticism.
Cortázar and Burroughs occupied the shared 1960s Paris avant-garde milieu, although no direct interaction is established.
Boal later adapted and directed Cortázar’s Nada más a Calingasta in Graz in 1981.
Bioy met and photographed Cortázar, and the two also engaged with each other’s writing publicly.
Cortázar visited revolutionary Cuba and interacted with its leadership while supporting and later critically engaging with the revolution.
Cortázar and Vicuña participated in the same 1974 Arts Festival for Democracy in Chile project, although no personal meeting is established.
Schávelzon discussed Cortázar’s subway fiction in interpreting Buenos Aires’s subterranean imaginary and tunnel legends.
Sartre and Cortázar belonged to a shared international left-intellectual milieu without a more specific documented life connection.
Cicero and Caesar corresponded during political and civil-war crises, including Caesar's attempts in 49 BCE to obtain Cicero's cooperation.
Cicero and Caesar knew and met each other personally over many years, including at Ravenna in 52 BCE.
Caesar and Cleopatra met at Alexandria in 48 BCE and became political and sexual partners who remained personally connected until his assassination.
Strabo wrote about the earlier Caesar's campaigns and their geographical consequences.
Pliny wrote about the earlier Caesar's abilities, military record, human cost, family traditions, and calendar.
Josephus wrote about the earlier Caesar's eastern settlement and reproduced documents attributed to him concerning Hyrcanus II and Jewish privileges.
Virgil represented the earlier, deceased Caesar in Augustan poetry through themes of divinity, civil war, and Julian genealogy.
Dante portrayed the earlier Caesar in the Divine Comedy, placing him in Limbo and treating his killing as an archetypal betrayal.
Napoleon dictated an extended strategic commentary on the earlier Caesar's campaigns.
Caesar reportedly visited Alexander's tomb in Alexandria long after Alexander's death.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Wells treated Caesar’s military career, dictatorship, assassination, and place in Rome’s transition from republic to empire in both *The Outline of History* and *A Short History of the World*. [Primary text](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/35461/35461-h/35461-h.htm)
Solinus wrote about Julius Caesar’s calendar reform, giraffe exhibition, remarkable horse, and dedication of a pearl breastplate.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Vigenère translated and extensively annotated Caesar’s *Commentaries*, with editions culminating in the expanded 1589 Paris publication. He also discussed Caesar’s substitution method in the *Traicté des chiffres*. [Bibliothèque de Genève catalogue and digitization](https://www.e-rara.ch/gep_g/content/titleinfo/1752481); [primary-text transcription, fol. 11v](https://wulfric.artsci.utoronto.ca/rentexte/vigenere/chif_traite.htm)

- **[T1-]** Dickens wrote about Caesar’s expeditions to Britain in the opening chapter of *A Child’s History of England*, serialized in 1851–53. **Documented fact.** [Primary text](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/699/699-h/699-h.htm)
Paul narrated Caesar’s civil war, victory over Pompey, Alexandrian campaign, relationship with Cleopatra, and later wars.
D’Annunzio appropriated Caesarian authority and Roman imperial imagery in his political rhetoric.
Some Huon de Bordeaux genealogies place Morgan and Julius Caesar within the same fantastical family milieu through the fairy king Oberon.
Yarvin wrote about Caesar as a historical model for concentrated personal authority and elite-popular political alignment.
Later military literature placed Hannibal and Caesar together in a comparative canon of exemplary commanders.
Bazeries later discussed substitution cryptography associated with Julius Caesar in Les Chiffres secrets dévoilés.
The later Caesar promoted the legendary claim that his lineage descended from Aeneas and depicted Aeneas carrying Anchises and the Palladium on denarii.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Quintilian evaluates Julius Caesar as both writer and orator. In the Roman prose canon he praises Caesar’s force, acuteness, energy, and stylistic elegance and judges that, had Caesar devoted himself principally to advocacy, he could have rivaled Cicero. This is retrospective literary criticism, written more than a century after Caesar’s death. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html)
Dumas portrayed Julius Caesar in the popular biographical-historical work César.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** In *The Goddess of Atvatabar* (New York, 1892), Bradshaw has narrator Lexington White tell Lyone about “Caesar” while recounting the grandeur of Rome; the pairing with Hannibal, Cleopatra, and Antony contextually identifies Julius Caesar. This is a brief fictional-historical reference, not evidence of deeper study or influence. [Project Gutenberg text, chapter XXII](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/32825/32825-h/32825-h.htm)
Royer depicted Caesar receiving the surrender of Vercingetorix in an 1899 painting.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact.** Kerckhoffs described Caesar’s reported use of a shifted alphabet for private correspondence and explained why simple alphabetic substitutions were commonly called the “method of Julius Caesar.” His account relied explicitly on Suetonius and Aulus Gellius. ([Part I](https://www.petitcolas.net/kerckhoffs/la_cryptographie_militaire_i.htm))
After Evola's death, Dugin translated, circulated, and interpreted Evola's writings and incorporated elements of his Traditionalism into his own thought.
Evola critically discussed Besant's Theosophical leadership and her promotion of Jiddu Krishnamurti as a World Teacher.
Evola critically examined Helena P. Blavatsky's Theosophy while drawing on or paralleling aspects of its prehistoric and cyclical cosmology.
Evola interpreted Dante as an initiate and representative of the Ghibelline imperial current.
Evola read d’Annunzio closely and later criticized the D’Annunzian conception of the superman.
Evola entered Marinetti's Futurist circle and participated in its artistic activity, supporting a personal acquaintance but not a close friendship.
Evola appropriated and revised Johann Gottlieb Fichte's absolute idealism while developing his own magical idealism.
Evola criticized Freud's accounts of the unconscious and sexuality as reductive and subpersonal.
Evola critically discussed Gurdjieff's discipline and doctrine of awakening while rejecting his movement as an adequate initiatic authority.
Evola engaged and sought to move beyond Hegelian idealism through his concept of an operatively powerful absolute individual.
Evola discussed both Krishnamurti's promotion as World Teacher and his later rejection of that role, treating the latter with qualified respect.
Evola engaged Jung's psychology and considered it less reductive than Freud's while rejecting its psychologization of metaphysical and initiatic symbols.
Evola and Eliade met in Bucharest in 1937 and twice in postwar Rome, alongside an intermittent correspondence and literary cooperation that later ended in estrangement.
Mussolini personally received Evola at the Palazzo Venezia in September 1941 to discuss Evola's racial-doctrine book.
Evola repeatedly interpreted and criticized Nietzsche's ideas, including nihilism, eternal recurrence, the Übermensch, and the will to power.
Evola identified Wilde as one of the writers who shaped his adolescent revolt against bourgeois life and conventional morality.
Evola and Guénon maintained substantial correspondence and debated questions of metaphysics, initiation, political action, and spiritual authority.
Evola critically examined Steiner's Anthroposophy while also drawing on themes circulating through Anthroposophical associates.
Evola contributed extensively to Tucci's IsMEO publishing environment and submitted at least one article directly to him by letter.
Serrano credibly reported visiting Evola at his Rome apartment in 1970 and conversing with him there.
Serrano engaged textually with a Traditionalist and tantric milieu shaped by Evola, without a documented meeting or direct correspondence.

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** They maintained an intermittent correspondence from the interwar period, re-established it in September 1949, reviewed and cited one another’s work, and discussed yoga, Tantra, esotericism, translations, racism, and fascism. Their relationship suffered ruptures in 1955 and 1964 and should not be described as an uncomplicated friendship. [Liviu Bordaș, “The Difficult Encounter in Rome”](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/369236062_The_difficult_encounter_in_Rome_Mircea_Eliade%27s_post-war_relation_with_Julius_Evola_-_new_letters_and_data_International_Journal_on_Humanistic_Ideology_IV_no_2_Autumn-Winter_2011_pp_125-158)
Evola participated in the postwar Futurist milieu associated with Marinetti before rejecting his leadership and ideology.
Evola selectively appropriated Nietzsche within aristocratic and anti-modern political thought.
Savitri Devi's later Traditionalist framework drew to some degree on Evola's ideas, without a documented personal meeting or correspondence.

counterpart_name: Abu Yazid Tayfur ibn Isa al-Bistami
text: Junayd reportedly translated, explained, or commented on ecstatic sayings attributed to Abu Yazid.
Early traditions report a temporary personal association in Baghdad during which Junayd counseled al-Hallaj and later distanced himself from him.

counterpart_name: Abu al-Qasim Abd al-Karim ibn Hawazin al-Qushayri
text: Al-Qushayri extensively quoted and canonized the earlier Junayd in the Risala.
Later Qadiri chains and literature presented Junayd as a central predecessor.
Attar wrote about the earlier Junayd in Tadhkirat al-awliya through sayings, teaching stories, and miracle narratives.
Ibn Arabi cited the earlier Junayd as an authoritative knower.
Rumi participated in a later Persian Sufi literary tradition that transmitted Junayd's authority, anecdotes, and sayings.
Junayd grounded his teachings in the Quran and the prophetic Sunna associated with Muhammad.
Later Sufi genealogies placed Junayd in a spiritual lineage traced through the earlier Abu Bakr.
Later Chishti genealogies incorporated the earlier Junayd into the prehistory of their initiatic tradition.
Later Chishti genealogies incorporated the earlier Junayd into the prehistory of their initiatic tradition.
Some later Naqshbandi genealogies included Junayd among their formative predecessors.
Baha ud-Din Walad belonged to a later Persian Sufi environment in which Junayd was received as a canonical authority.
Shams al-Din Muhammad of Tabriz belonged to a later Persian Sufi environment in which Junayd was received as a canonical authority.
Buber treated this earlier Islamic mystic within his comparative survey of mystical testimony.
Later Qādirī initiatic chains connect al-Jīlānī backward to al-Junayd, although the accuracy of each intermediate link remains uncertain.
Al-Junayd posthumously described Ibrahim as possessing the key to the knowledge or sciences of the Sufi path.
Jung was the later namesake and paternal descendant of the elder Carl Gustav Jung, with Basel serving as a shared family setting across generations.
Jung was Preiswerk’s later maternal descendant and inherited family stories associated with his grandfather’s Basel household.
Jung personally met Freud and became his correspondent, collaborator, institutional ally, protégé, and later theoretical rival.
James influenced Jung intellectually, and a personal encounter connected with Jung’s 1909 American visit is reported but less fully documented.
Einstein visited Jung’s Zurich home several times before the First World War and discussed relativity with him.
Pauli was Jung’s analytic case, correspondent, and collaborator on dreams, number, matter, psyche, and synchronicity.
Dulles received Jung’s wartime psychological assessments of Hitler, Nazi leaders, and German political behavior.
Jung analyzed Gross at the Burghölzli and engaged in an intensive personal exchange with him in 1908.
Jung participated as a lecturer in the milieu of Keyserling’s School of Wisdom in Darmstadt.
Jung met Fröbe-Kapteyn around 1930 and subsequently became a central Eranos lecturer and adviser under her leadership.
Eliade met and conversed with Jung as a fellow Eranos lecturer at Ascona.
Buber and Jung participated in the same broader Eranos and comparative-religion intellectual network, although sustained direct collaboration was not established.
Tucci and Jung occupied the shared institutional milieu of Eranos at Ascona without a major bilateral collaboration being established.
Hesse met Jung after undergoing analysis with a Jungian therapist, and Jung also commented on Hesse’s work.
Serrano visited and corresponded with Jung during the 1950s and later published an account of their friendship.
Jung was the later thinker who lectured extensively on Nietzsche and interpreted him as both a psychological thinker and a case of archetypal identification.
Jung engaged deeply with Goethe’s work, especially Faust, while the alleged biological family connection remained only a rumor.
Jung engaged with Kant’s philosophy as a major influence on his distinction between experience and unknowable reality.
Jung was the later author who studied Paracelsus as a precursor of psychologically significant alchemy and wrote multiple essays about him.
Jung engaged with Boehme’s symbolic theology in his study of Western religious and alchemical traditions.
Jung engaged with Swedenborg’s visionary and theological ideas in investigating spiritualism, visions, and religious experience.
Jung and Gräser belonged to the broader Ascona and Monte Verità regional-intellectual environment, while claims of a secret teacher-student relationship remain unsubstantiated.
Jung had documented professional contact with Joyce's family through his examination or treatment of Lucia Joyce and his comments about Lucia and her father.
Jung later reproduced and cited imagery from works attributed to Trismosin in his twentieth-century alchemical studies.

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Jung recalled reading seven volumes of Swedenborg while studying occult and paranormal literature during his university years, and he referred to Swedenborg in later autobiographical and psychological discussions. Claims that Jung’s mature psychology was simply derived from Swedenborg go beyond this evidence. [Jung, *Memories, Dreams, Reflections* text](https://ratical.org/co-globalize/MemoriesDreamsReflections-Jung.pdf), [Swedenborg Society reception summary](https://www.swedenborg.org.uk/events/swedenborg-and-the-english-romantics-items-from-the-swedenborg-collection/)
Ritsema later wrote about Carl Gustav Jung as a formative figure in Eranos history and recounted Jung’s reported response to an earlier proposal for experiential work with the I Ching.
Dick extensively read Jung and drew on Jungian concepts when interpreting his dreams and 2-3-74.
Jung engaged Christian-alchemical symbolism associated with Böhme’s later reception, although Jung’s Aurora Consurgens is distinct from Böhme’s Aurora.
Herbert engaged with Jungian psychology through Irene and Ralph Slattery, including ideas about the collective unconscious and archetypal or inherited memory.
Guénon’s account of sacred, supra-human symbolism stood in documented intellectual opposition to Jungian psychological explanations of symbols.
Fortune studied Jung's psychology and adapted ideas resembling archetypes and the collective unconscious in her occult explanations.
Pauli corresponded with Jung for roughly twenty-five years and co-published Naturerklärung und Psyche with him.
Dugin published, translated, and discussed Jung as a central figure of soft Traditionalism, the Eranos milieu, and the modern Dionysian Logos.
Evola engaged Jung's psychology and considered it less reductive than Freud's while rejecting its psychologization of metaphysical and initiatic symbols.

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Eliade interviewed Jung at the August 1952 Eranos conference for the French newspaper *Combat*. Their surviving exchanges and Eliade’s later writings document both intellectual engagement and occasional tension over the distinction between Jung’s psychological archetypes and Eliade’s historical-religious morphology. [*C. G. Jung Speaking: Interviews and Encounters*](https://jungiancenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/cg-jung-speaking.pdf)
Breton knew Jungian concepts while favoring Freud, but no personal meeting or collaboration was documented.
Carl Gustav Jung later wrote about Dr Carl Jung of Mainz as a purported paternal ancestor while acknowledging that the descent was unproven.
Lacan discussed Jung in his accounts of psychoanalytic history without becoming a Jungian disciple.
Jung cited Blake and reproduced Blake’s images in Psychology and Alchemy.
Spinetta engaged with Jung’s writings and drew recurring psychological and symbolic influence from them.
Fromm examined and contrasted Jung's archetypal theory of dreams and myths with Freudian and historical-humanistic interpretations.
Jung occasionally used Aristotelian concepts transmitted through scholastic and alchemical traditions.
Cirlot explicitly drew on Jung’s writings about alchemy and depth psychology when explaining the basis of his symbol dictionary.

- **[T1+]** Jung repeatedly engaged the earlier Simon in seminars and writings; in *Collected Works* 18 he addressed the figure concealed in his visionary Philemon as “Simon Magus,” while his 1931 *Visions Seminar* discussed Simon as the legendary arch-heretic and father of Gnosis. Jung’s written engagement is **documented fact**; the visionary identification of Philemon with Simon belongs to Jung’s personal symbolic experience, not historical biography. [Jung quotation from *Collected Works* 18](https://carljungdepthpsychologysite.blog/2021/09/06/world-10/)
Dulles met Carl Gustav Jung repeatedly in wartime Switzerland and consulted him about Hitler's psychology and probable behavior.

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** In *Psychologie consonantiste* (1938), Odobleja named Jung alongside Freud, Adler, Bleuler, and others within his critical classification of contemporary psychologies of the unconscious. The evidence supports one-sided textual engagement only; no meeting or correspondence between Jung and Odobleja has been identified. [Digitized volume and indexed passage](https://www.scribd.com/document/472087793/Psychologie-consonantiste-vol-I-1938)
Jung and Jungian writers interpreted the reported dreams of Descartes as psychologically and symbolically significant.

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Jung incorporated the alchemical *Aurora consurgens*, then attributed to Thomas, into his psychological study of alchemy and arranged for Marie-Louise von Franz to edit and comment upon it as a companion volume to *Mysterium Coniunctionis*. The engagement is real, but its premise is an **allegation or theory**: modern catalogues generally classify the *Aurora* as Pseudo-Aquinas rather than an authentic work by Thomas. [Durham University thesis repository](https://etheses.durham.ac.uk/id/eprint/14918/1/UNIO_MYSTICA_AND_THE_AURORA_CONSURGENS_%28CORRECTED%29.pdf), [Aurora Consurgens project](https://auroraconsurgens.org/about/)
Jung's later work incorporated Fludd's images and the Kepler–Fludd controversy into his interpretation of alchemical and intellectual history.
Jung and Jungian interpreters used alchemical and descent imagery associated with interpretations of Dante.
Jung’s work appeared within the Sur publishing and intellectual network, although no close personal relationship with Ocampo is established.
Jung’s grandson later investigated his diaries and incorporated accounts of his grandfather into his autobiographical self-understanding.
Jung posthumously wrote about Preiswerk, his maternal grandfather, as a visionary figure in his psychiatric and autobiographical accounts.
Jung's intellectual engagement with Grail symbolism helped bring the earlier Parzival tradition into analytical-psychological interpretation.
Mesmer’s magnetic legacy formed part of the mediated cultural background of hypnosis, dissociation, occult experimentation, and psychical research in which Jung’s psychology developed.
Culianu wrote about Jung’s psychology of religion and archetypes, ultimately rejecting archetypes as an adequate historical explanation.
Jung posthumously interpreted Goethe’s Faust, alchemical themes, and symbolic ancestry claims.
Žižek critically contrasts his Lacanian orientation with Jung's archetypal psychology.
Biographical accounts report a professional connection in which Jung referred patients to Perrottet, although the precise relationship remains unresolved.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas treated Aristotle’s philosophy and its reception in medieval theology at length in *Auch eine Geschichte der Philosophie* (2019), including a section titled “The Challenges Posed by Aristotle for Thirteenth-Century Theology.” [Habermas Forum contents](https://www.habermasforum.dk/news-139/out-now-in-english-quotalso-a-history-of-philosophyquot-volume-1)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** *Auch eine Geschichte der Philosophie* contains an extended treatment of Augustine and the institutional development of the Latin Church; Habermas also explicitly classified Augustine among the major metaphysical thinkers discussed in his account of postmetaphysical philosophy. [Habermas Forum contents](https://www.habermasforum.dk/news-139/out-now-in-english-quotalso-a-history-of-philosophyquot-volume-1), [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas critically appropriated Austin’s speech-act theory while developing universal/formal pragmatics during the 1970s, particularly the distinction among locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts. This was textual engagement; Austin died in 1960, and no meeting is documented. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas wrote directly about Benjamin in “Bewußtmachende oder rettende Kritik—die Aktualität Walter Benjamins” (1972), subsequently collected in *Philosophisch-politische Profile*. [Suhrkamp](https://www.suhrkamp.de/buch/juergen-habermas-philosophisch-politische-profile-t-9783518282595), [MIT Press edition contents](https://books.google.com/books/about/Philosophical_political_Profiles.html?id=ICtx4qVgUoUC)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas repeatedly engaged Dewey’s pragmatism, democratic theory, and model of a problem-solving public, especially in reconstructing communicative rationality and deliberative democracy. The connection is intellectual rather than personal; Dewey died in 1952, before Habermas’s academic career was established. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** After Habermas’s sustained criticism of Derrida in *Der philosophische Diskurs der Moderne* (1985), the two reconciled personally in the late 1990s, held a joint Frankfurt seminar in 2000, and cooperated against the Iraq War in 2003. Derrida expressly endorsed Habermas’s “15 February” European manifesto, and their later relationship is documented as a friendship lasting until Derrida’s death in 2004. [Wiley contents](https://www.wiley-vch.de/en?isbn=9780745608303&option=com_eshop&title=The+Philosophical+Discourse+of+Modernity&view=product), [Derrida–Habermas Reader](https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.3366/j.ctvxcrk9s)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas discussed Fichte as part of the post-Kantian development of German idealism and the genealogy of reason, subjectivity, and freedom, most extensively in the historical reconstruction culminating in *Auch eine Geschichte der Philosophie*. The record supports intellectual treatment, not personal crossing.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas devoted substantial portions of *Der philosophische Diskurs der Moderne*—including “Some Questions Concerning the Theory of Power: Foucault Again”—to Foucault’s genealogy, theory of power, and normative position. The often-invoked “Habermas–Foucault debate” was principally a textual controversy; the projected direct encounter did not occur before Foucault’s death in 1984. [Wiley contents](https://www.wiley-vch.de/en?isbn=9780745608303&option=com_eshop&title=The+Philosophical+Discourse+of+Modernity&view=product), [Habermas bibliography](https://philarchive.org/archive/CORJHA)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas reconstructed Freud’s psychoanalysis as a model of emancipatory self-reflection in *Erkenntnis und Interesse* (1968), while criticizing Freud’s scientistic self-understanding. Freud died in 1939; no personal contact is possible. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Hegel is a major object of Habermas’s writing across *Erkenntnis und Interesse*, *Der philosophische Diskurs der Moderne*, and *Auch eine Geschichte der Philosophie*. The latter includes “Hegel’s Assimilation of Faith and Knowledge,” while the 1985 lectures begin their genealogy of philosophical modernity with Hegel. [Habermas Forum contents](https://www.habermasforum.dk/news-139/out-now-in-english-quotalso-a-history-of-philosophyquot-volume-1), [Wiley](https://www.wiley-vch.de/en?isbn=9780745608303&option=com_eshop&title=The+Philosophical+Discourse+of+Modernity&view=product)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Habermas publicly challenged Heidegger in 1953 over the unrevised reappearance of the phrase about the “inner truth and greatness” of National Socialism in *Einführung in die Metaphysik*. Heidegger answered privately through the *Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung*, making this a documented written exchange. Habermas later published further essays on Heidegger and devoted a lecture of *Der philosophische Diskurs der Moderne* to his critique of Western rationalism. [Suhrkamp](https://www.suhrkamp.de/buch/juergen-habermas-philosophisch-politische-profile-t-9783518282595), [Wiley](https://www.wiley-vch.de/en?isbn=9780745608303&option=com_eshop&title=The+Philosophical+Discourse+of+Modernity&view=product)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Horkheimer was Habermas’s senior colleague and institutional antagonist at Frankfurt’s Institute for Social Research in 1956–1959. Their relationship included direct correspondence: the Horkheimer archive records a 1955 letter with Habermas’s reply. Horkheimer subsequently opposed publication of *Student und Politik* and Habermas’s Frankfurt habilitation, although the two later partially reconciled. [Hessian archival catalogue](https://arcinsys.hessen.de/arcinsys/showArchivalDescriptionDetails?archivalDescriptionId=4039486), [Suhrkamp](https://www.suhrkamp.de/buch/juergen-habermas-philosophisch-politische-profile-t-9783518282595)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas engaged James as part of the American-pragmatist tradition used to reconstruct knowledge, action, and intersubjective reason. No personal crossing was possible: James died in 1910.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Kant is one of Habermas’s most persistent historical interlocutors. Habermas discussed Kantian autonomy, practical reason, publicity, cosmopolitanism, and the translation of religious concepts into postmetaphysical philosophy; *Auch eine Geschichte der Philosophie* includes “Kant’s Answer to Hume.” [Habermas Forum contents](https://www.habermasforum.dk/news-139/out-now-in-english-quotalso-a-history-of-philosophyquot-volume-1), [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas explicitly situated Leibniz within the metaphysical tradition reconstructed and criticized in his accounts of postmetaphysical thinking. This is documented textual engagement, not a biographical crossing. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas devoted a substantial part of *Auch eine Geschichte der Philosophie* to Luther’s break with scholastic tradition and its consequences for faith, freedom, and modern law. [Habermas Forum contents](https://www.habermasforum.dk/news-139/out-now-in-english-quotalso-a-history-of-philosophyquot-volume-1)

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Habermas and Marcuse were personally acquainted, corresponded, and remained friendly despite disagreements over the West German student movement. Habermas visited Marcuse in hospital at Starnberg shortly before Marcuse’s death on 29 July 1979 and later reported their final conversation about compassion as critical theory’s normative basis. Habermas also published “Herbert Marcuse über Kunst und Revolution” (1973). [Suhrkamp](https://www.suhrkamp.de/buch/juergen-habermas-philosophisch-politische-profile-t-9783518282595), [Adorno–Marcuse correspondence](https://newleftreview.org/issues/i233/articles/theodor-adorno-herbert-marcuse-correspondence-on-the-german-student-movement.pdf)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas wrote extensively about Marx from his 1950s literature review on Marxism through *Erkenntnis und Interesse*, *Zur Rekonstruktion des Historischen Materialismus*, and *Theorie des kommunikativen Handelns*. His project explicitly sought to reconstruct Marxian social criticism while rejecting labor reductionism, historical inevitability, and the proletariat’s privileged epistemic status. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas treated Nietzsche in *Erkenntnis und Interesse* and made him the pivotal figure of “The Entry into Postmodernity: Nietzsche as a Turning Point” in *Der philosophische Diskurs der Moderne*. [Wiley contents](https://www.wiley-vch.de/en?isbn=9780745608303&option=com_eshop&title=The+Philosophical+Discourse+of+Modernity&view=product)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas discussed Plato as a foundational representative of metaphysical philosophy in his contrast between classical metaphysics and postmetaphysical reason. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas’s 1954 Bonn dissertation, *Das Absolute und die Geschichte. Von der Zwiespältigkeit in Schellings Denken*, was an extended study of Schelling’s philosophy of history and the absolute. He returned to Schelling in later genealogical work. [Heidelberg University Library digitization](https://digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de/diglit/habermas1954), [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Habermas engaged Searle’s reformulation of speech-act theory in developing formal pragmatics and later exchanged published arguments with him concerning meaning, intentionality, and communicative action. The evidence supports written intellectual discourse; no independently verified personal friendship is asserted here. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** *Auch eine Geschichte der Philosophie* contains an extended section on Aquinas’s response to Aristotelian philosophy and the medieval synthesis of faith and knowledge. [Habermas Forum contents](https://www.habermasforum.dk/news-139/out-now-in-english-quotalso-a-history-of-philosophyquot-volume-1)

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Habermas met Adorno in 1955 and served as his research assistant at Frankfurt’s Institute for Social Research from 1956 to 1959. Adorno became his principal early mentor and institutional defender. Habermas later wrote several studies of Adorno, delivered the 1980 Adorno Prize lecture, and reconstructed critical theory partly through disagreement with Adorno’s philosophy of reason. [Suhrkamp](https://www.suhrkamp.de/buch/juergen-habermas-philosophisch-politische-profile-t-9783518282595), [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Habermas made Weber’s theory of rationalization a central object of *Theorie des kommunikativen Handelns* (1981), adopting Weber’s diagnosis of modern differentiation while criticizing its restriction of rationality to purposive and value-rational action. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/habermas/)
Buber became an earlier figure addressed within Habermas’s later philosophical reception context.
Habermas reviewed Heidegger’s Introduction to Metaphysics in 1953 and criticized its unretracted National Socialist language.
Karp interacted personally with Habermas while studying in Frankfurt, although Habermas was not his formal doctoral supervisor.
Habermas worked in later philosophical traditions shaped by Rousseauian problems without being established as Rousseau's direct disciple.

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Habermas worked as a research assistant at the Frankfurt Institute in the **1950s** and knew Horkheimer personally. Horkheimer regarded parts of Habermas’s Marxist political writing as too radical and impeded his advancement at Frankfurt, contributing to Habermas’s move to Marburg. “Friendship” would overstate the evidence; the supported connection is personal acquaintance within a hierarchical institutional relationship.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** James read Kant during his formative years and repeatedly discussed Kantian categories, the transcendental ego, rationalism, and the limits of conceptual thought. *The Varieties of Religious Experience* explicitly treats Kant’s depersonalization of the transcendental ego, while James’s later pluralism and radical empiricism were partly constructed against post-Kantian intellectualism. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/james/), [*The Varieties of Religious Experience*](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/621/621-h/621-h.html)
Buber read Kant during a youthful philosophical crisis and drew on his treatment of knowledge and reason.
Austin engaged with Kant as a significant subject of his formative philosophical study.
Schiller engaged directly in writing with Kant’s aesthetics and ethics, although no personal meeting between them is established.
Kant wrote to Bode in 1790 about cosmological priority and Saturn's ring, and Bode published the communication.
Bode cited Kant's cosmological work in editions of his own astronomical manual and helped broaden its readership.
Kant sent Euler his first publication and later engaged in writing with Euler’s natural philosophy and logical diagrams.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Kant was the subject of Horkheimer’s **1922 doctorate**, *Zur Antinomie der teleologischen Urteilskraft*, and his **1925 habilitation**, *Über Kants Kritik der Urteilskraft als Bindeglied zwischen theoretischer und praktischer Philosophie*. The familiar titles “Karl Marx ha muerto” and “A la muerte de Karl Marx” are later editorial shorthand: the passage originally formed part of a broader “Cartas de Martí” chronicle. [Publication-history discussion](https://jovencuba.com/marx-textos-marti/), [contemporary-text reproduction](https://www.yumpu.com/es/document/view/14540183/cartas-de-marti-la-nacion-buenos-aires-portal-jose-marti)

text: Beauvoir engaged with Marx’s historical materialism through his writings rather than through a personal meeting.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Wells repeatedly analyzed and criticized Marx’s doctrines, historical method, class analysis, and political afterlife. Extended treatments appear in *The Outline of History*, *The Work, Wealth and Happiness of Mankind*, *The Open Conspiracy*, and the published 1934 Stalin–Wells discussion. Wells identified as a socialist but rejected Marxist orthodoxy and class dictatorship.

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Marx repeatedly discussed Garibaldi in contemporary newspaper articles and private correspondence. His **23 July 1860** article analyzed Garibaldi’s rupture with Giuseppe La Farina using the contents of a Garibaldi letter supplied by a London intermediary; in an **19 April 1864** letter to Engels, Marx sharply criticized Garibaldi’s London politics. This was one-sided written engagement: no reliable evidence establishes correspondence or a personal meeting between them. [Marx’s 1860 article](https://marxengels.public-archives.com/en/ME1208en.html), [Marx’s 1864 letter](https://marx-ebooks.github.io/en/MECW/41/MECW41-311.html)

Land engaged critically with Marx’s analysis of capital while rejecting conventional emancipatory Marxism.

Karp, born long after Marx's death, engaged with Marxist theories of alienated labor and Marxian intellectual traditions.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** In “The Straussian Moment,” Thiel placed Marx and Smith on opposing political sides but argued that both ultimately treated people as rational economic actors, a premise he considered insufficient. [Essay text](https://www.vigneshatm.com/Compendia/2007-the-straussian-moment-thiel.pdf)

- **[T1-]** Haraway repeatedly engaged Marx’s categories of labor, production, capital, class, and technological transformation, most conspicuously in “‘Gender’ for a Marxist Dictionary” and “A Manifesto for Cyborgs” (1985). The latter deliberately reworked the manifesto form for socialist-feminist politics while criticizing Marxist traditions that inadequately explained gendered, racialized, reproductive, and informational labor. This is a **documented fact**, not a claim of doctrinal Marxism or personal connection ([original manifesto text](https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/donna-haraway-a-cyborg-manifesto); [Encyclopedia of Anthropology](https://ea.fflch.usp.br/en/node/61)).
Salomon’s son Dagobert helped establish the Rheinische Zeitung before it later employed Marx as editor, creating an indirect posthumous institutional link.
Castro engaged with Marx through writings that became a central intellectual source of his declared Marxism-Leninism.

The connection is posthumous intellectual commentary; no meeting or correspondence between Brown and Marx is documented. [Pliny, *Natural History* 6](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0137%3Abook%3D6&force=y), [8.14](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0137%3Abook%3D8%3Achapter%3D14)

- **[T9+]** **Documented fact:** Pataliputra is a shared site without shared occupancy. There is no evidence that Xuanzang possessed or consulted Megasthenes’ text, so the connection is limited to the same historically changing site. Spinetta discussed Foucault and drew on his ideas about the body, soul, discipline, and violence around Téster de violencia.
The later Foucault interpreted Aristotle within his histories of ancient ethics and practices of the self.

Cornelius consciously engaged with Michelangelo’s monumental art when developing his own forms and the Ludwigskirche Last Judgment.
Michelangelo portrayed Anthony in the early painting traditionally known as the Torment of Saint Anthony.
Dumas wrote a popular biographical treatment of Michelangelo in Michel-Ange et Raphaël Sanzio.

Nietzsche read Don Quixote and engaged with Cervantes in letters, notes, and philosophical writings over several decades.

Viladrich later encountered Cervantes through childhood reading of Don Quijote and through his family home’s Cervantine name.

Girard treated Cervantes as one of the novelists who reveal that supposedly autonomous desire is mediated by another. [Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://iep.utm.edu/girard/)
Hugo invoked this earlier figure as a literary authority and associated the figure with the purported communications of the Jersey séances.
Cervantes engaged the chivalric-romance culture through which stories of Lancelot circulated, without treating Lancelot as a uniquely established model.
Critical accounts identify Cervantes as a literary precedent in Jarry’s reading and treatment of comic pseudo-history.
Spence discussed Cervantes's literary development, his judgment of Palmerin of England, and Don Quixote.
Gerchunoff repeatedly wrote about Cervantes's Don Quixote as a literary model and ethical archetype.
Bakunin met Marx, corresponded with him, translated part of Capital, and later became his rival within the First International.

Bakunin translated the earlier philosopher Fichte and was influenced by his ideas about moral vocation and action.
Bakunin read and discussed Kant during his early philosophical development.
Bakunin read Schelling and personally attended his lectures in Berlin.
Bakunin later engaged and criticized ideas about freedom, society, authority, and the state associated with the earlier thinker Rousseau.
Bakunin treated the earlier socialist Fourier as a significant predecessor while engaging Fourierist ideas.
Bakunin studied and criticized the ideas of the earlier socialist Saint-Simon.
Bakunin visited Garibaldi at Caprera, received introductions from him, corresponded with him, and later criticized his political compromises.
Bakunin repeatedly met Wagner while both participated in the Dresden revolutionary movement of May 1849.
Hugo and Bakunin belonged to the broad organizational milieu of the League of Peace and Freedom, although no direct meeting was verified.
Bakunin was an earlier figure received within the revolutionary tradition inherited by Sorel.
Camus discussed the earlier Bakunin and his relationship to revolutionary nihilism in The Rebel.
Chomsky later identified with the libertarian-socialist and anarcho-syndicalist tradition in which Bakunin is a canonical predecessor.
Antoinette and Richard occupied Villa Baronata in 1883–84, after the property had previously been associated with Bakunin, who died before they lived there.

Luxemburg critically discussed Bakunin's political legacy and distinguished revolutionary mass strikes from the Bakuninist conception of a general strike.
Pouget retrospectively situated libertarian socialism within the Bakuninist side of the First International's conflict with Marx.
Rothbard discussed Bakunin as part of the collectivist anarchist tradition that he rejected.
Landauer drew on Bakunin’s anti-statism while rejecting insurrectionary and purely destructive interpretations of anarchism.
Mühsam read Bakunin and adopted elements of his anti-state revolutionary anarchism without ever having personal contact.
Bakunin and Kierkegaard were both present as auditors at Schelling's inaugural Berlin lecture in November 1841.
Puckette portrayed Cage in his 2016 installation Four Sound Portraits as one of the four composers he most admired.

The Milton Friedman Prize for Advancing Liberty connects Friedman as its namesake, who authorized the use of his name, with Charles Koch as a later recipient.

Rothbard knew Friedman through postwar free-market circles while repeatedly opposing his economic theories and policy proposals.
Varoufakis engaged Friedman’s monetarism, crowding-out argument, and proposal for a form of universal basic income.

After returning to Bucharest, he spoke on “India” at Criterion’s Gandhi symposium on 10 December 1932 and repeatedly discussed Gandhi’s anticolonial movement in his journalism and memoirs. [Cristina A. Bejan, *Intellectuals and Fascism in Interwar Romania*](https://dokumen.pub/intellectuals-and-fascism-in-interwar-romania-the-criterion-association-3030201643-9783030201647.html)

They later encountered one another in European Orientalist circles and both lectured at Eranos in Ascona; the evidence supports a long collegial relationship, not a formal teacher–student one. - **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Eliade first attended Fröbe-Kapteyn’s Eranos gathering at Casa Gabriella near Ascona in August 1950 and returned repeatedly. She served as his host, editor, and network broker, including in connections leading toward Bollingen support. [Fondazione Eranos publications and records](https://eranosfoundation.org/PRE/publications_b.htm)
- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Eliade met Jung through Eranos at Ascona beginning in 1950 and participated with him in the conference milieu during several later sessions.

Their surviving exchanges and Eliade’s later writings document both intellectual engagement and occasional tension over the distinction between Jung’s psychological archetypes and Eliade’s historical-religious morphology. [*C. G. Jung Speaking: Interviews and Encounters*](https://jungiancenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/cg-jung-speaking.pdf)
- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Eliade met Evola during Evola’s 1937 visit to Bucharest and met him again in Rome in May 1952 and April 1955.

Their relationship suffered ruptures in 1955 and 1964 and should not be described as an uncomplicated friendship. [Liviu Bordaș, “The Difficult Encounter in Rome”](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/369236062_The_difficult_encounter_in_Rome_Mircea_Eliade%27s_post-war_relation_with_Julius_Evola_-_new_letters_and_data_International_Journal_on_Humanistic_Ideology_IV_no_2_Autumn-Winter_2011_pp_125-158)

Guénon also acted as an epistolary intermediary in 1949 by supplying Evola with Eliade’s address, after which Evola resumed writing to him; no securely documented personal meeting between Eliade and Guénon was located. [Bordaș, “The Difficult Encounter in Rome”](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/369236062_The_difficult_encounter_in_Rome_Mircea_Eliade%27s_post-war_relation_with_Julius_Evola_-_new_letters_and_data_International_Journal_on_Humanistic_Ideology_IV_no_2_Autumn-Winter_2011_pp_125-158)

([Société des Amis d’Alfred Jarry](https://www.alfredjarry.fr/amisjarry/fichiers_ea/etoile_absinthe_091_92reduit.pdf), [critical discussion of *Messaline*](https://www.enotes.com/topics/alfred-jarry/criticism/jarry-alfred/keith-beaumont-essay-date-1984))

Cortés subsequently resided in the city, held Motecuhzoma under coercive Spanish control, and dealt with him repeatedly until the ruler’s death in late June 1520. The meeting is described in Cortés’s own *Second Letter* and in Indigenous and Spanish traditions, although their reported dialogue is disputed. [American Historical Association primary-source edition](https://www.historians.org/resource/cortes-on-meeting-moctezuma/), [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/item/2021667098/)
- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Cortés wrote extensively about Motecuhzoma—his court, dominions, reception of the Spaniards, captivity, and death—in the *Second Letter to Charles V*, signed **30 October 1520**. The connection is certain, though the letter’s claims about voluntary submission and responsibility for Motecuhzoma’s death are partisan and contested. [Early Americas Digital Archive](https://eada.lib.umd.edu/text-entries/second-letter-of-hernando-cortes-to-charles-v/)

His reconstruction depended on colonial histories and surviving material evidence rather than direct Indigenous testimony. [Cambridge University Press excerpt](https://assets.cambridge.org/97811080/77897/excerpt/9781108077897_excerpt.pdf), [Humboldt Studies journal](https://hin-online.de/index.php/hin/en/article/view/2)

The unrealized theatrical project presents him symbolically as the embodiment of a ritual and metaphysical Mexican order confronting Cortés, not as a historically exact portrait. [Revista de la Universidad de México](https://www.revistadelauniversidad.mx/articles/fe05e532-ce7a-40fc-926f-61cf4e67857c/la-conquista-de-mexico-(traduccion-de-enrique-flores))

Maduro joined Chávez’s movement, held several senior offices under him, and was publicly designated by Chávez as his successor.

Copernicus examined Aristotle’s arguments for a stationary central Earth, accepting parts of his physical tradition while rejecting geocentrism.
Copernicus discussed Plato’s arrangement of Mercury and Venus and invoked him when commenting on ancient astronomers.
Copernicus acknowledged that reading Cicero introduced him to Hicetas’s claim that Earth moved.

counterpart_name: Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci
text: Leonardo and Copernicus were both reportedly in Bologna during April 1500, although no interaction between them is established.
Luther reacted in remarks recorded in Table Talk to reports of Copernicus’s theory that Earth moves.
Bruno praised, criticized, and extended Copernicus’s ideas in The Ash Wednesday Supper.
Kepler repeatedly discussed and transformed Copernicus’s astronomical system in several works.
Galileo explicitly defended and developed Copernican terrestrial motion in several writings.
Descartes compared and critically adapted Copernicus’s system in Principles of Philosophy.
Huygens used Copernican planetary astronomy as the basis for discussing other inhabited worlds in Kosmotheoros.
Newton situated Copernicus in the history of planetary theory and supplied a mathematical dynamical framework for the Copernican system.
Kant invoked Copernicus’s reversal of the observer–heavens relationship as an analogy for changing philosophy’s method.
Bode's astronomical manuals presented the heliocentric planetary system inherited from Copernicus.

- **[T9-]** **Documented fact:** On 17 January 1614, while studying at Heidelberg, Comenius bought Copernicus’s autograph manuscript of *De revolutionibus* from the widow of mathematics professor Jakob Christmann. Comenius’s Latin ownership note survives in the codex. The manuscript subsequently passed through later collections and is now held by the Jagiellonian Library in Kraków. This is a direct shared-object connection: Copernicus originated the manuscript, and Comenius became a later owner. [Cambridge study noting the Heidelberg purchase](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-ecclesiastical-history/article/abs/irenicism-and-dogmatics-in-the-confessional-age-pareus-and-comenius-in-heidelberg-1614/6467FF3DC881970BE59D975411632D91); [Charles University study of the autograph’s provenance](https://dspace.cuni.cz/bitstream/handle/20.500.11956/53249/140026498.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=1)
Euler’s astronomical work proceeded from the heliocentric planetary theory associated with Copernicus.
Laplace retrospectively wrote about Copernicus and the establishment of the heliocentric system.
Hooke praised Copernicus as an exemplary discoverer and later sought observational evidence for Earth’s annual motion in the Copernican system.
Dee engaged textually with the mathematical astronomy in which Copernicus was a major reference, without simply adopting Copernicanism.
Yates analyzed Copernicus through Bruno’s partly Hermetic reception of heliocentrism in Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition.
Poulantzas extensively analyzed Gramsci’s concepts and his strategy and interpretation of Italian fascism.

Poulantzas discussed Trotsky’s positions on Comintern strategy, historical conditions, technology, and the challenges facing German and Italian Communists.

Poulantzas examined Mussolini’s tactics, political and class relationships, corporatism, party-building, and seizure of power.

Bohr corresponded and met repeatedly with Einstein, notably debating quantum completeness at the 1927 and 1930 Solvay Conferences and during the EPR controversy.

Bohr and Oppenheimer met through physics networks, worked together at Los Alamos, and discussed postwar international control.

Bohr and von Neumann shared the international mathematical-physics community and Manhattan Project environment, although close collaboration is not established.
Bohr and Curie moved in the same international physics and Solvay-conference milieu and attended major interwar scientific congresses.

Both also participated in the October 1927 Fifth Solvay Conference in Brussels. See the [University of Vienna archive catalogue](https://services.phaidra.univie.ac.at/api/object/o%3A2085354/download) and the [Solvay Institutes’ conference history](https://solvayinstitutes.be/conference/30th-solvay-conference-on-physics/).

Derrida wrote directly about Nietzsche's styles, gendered metaphors, and textual plurality.
Habermas critically presented Nietzsche as a pivotal figure in the philosophical discourse of modernity.
Adorno's critique of Enlightenment reason shared and critically transformed elements of Nietzschean genealogy.
Horkheimer's critique of Enlightenment reason shared and critically transformed elements of Nietzschean genealogy.
Benjamin worked within a German intellectual environment deeply shaped by Nietzsche, although the degree of direct influence is uncertain.
Hesse read and responded to Nietzschean individualism and cultural criticism.
Reference scholarship identifies Yeats as a writer significantly influenced by Nietzsche.
Nietzsche's Dionysianism and philosophy of dance entered the modern dance culture associated with Duncan, without a personal meeting.
Nietzsche's Dionysianism and philosophy of dance entered the modern dance culture associated with Wigman, without a personal meeting.

Searle discussed this earlier philosopher's ideas while addressing theories of mind, action, perception, reason, language, or social reality.
Barthes read Nietzsche from his youth and later adopted modes associated with Nietzsche’s work.

Spinetta engaged directly or indirectly with Nietzschean ideas concerning self-overcoming, values, and artistic transformation.
Critics identify Nietzsche’s writings as an intellectual source for Cirlot’s nihilism and Del no mundo.
Nietzsche later commented on the French literary culture of Hugo’s century, constituting reception rather than personal contact.
Nietzsche’s writings were reportedly carried in Guttzeit’s bookselling catalog, without evidence of a personal relationship.

counterpart_name: Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci
text: - **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** In a historical survey of movement science, Bernstein identified Leonardo da Vinci’s sixteenth-century investigations as an early, brilliant—but institutionally discontinuous—episode in the study of human movement. The passage appears in Bernstein’s posthumously translated writings. [Feigenberg, *Nikolai Bernstein: From Reflex to the Model of the Future*](https://dokumen.pub/nikolai-bernstein-from-reflex-to-the-model-of-the-future.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Bernstein wrote about Marey as a nineteenth-century precursor whose chronophotographic records constituted an exceptionally rich archive of movement, while arguing that the material had not yet yielded a continuing analytical research program. He also explicitly credited Marey’s use of instantaneous photography and point-tracking when explaining the technical ancestry of his own movement-recording methods. [Feigenberg, *Nikolai Bernstein: From Reflex to the Model of the Future*](https://dokumen.pub/nikolai-bernstein-from-reflex-to-the-model-of-the-future.html)

- **[T9-]** **Documented fact:** During his 1929 research journey, Bernstein visited the Institut Marey in Paris, an institution created to continue and standardize the motion-recording research originated by Marey. Marey had died in 1904, so this was not shared occupancy or a personal meeting; the institute and its technical legacy are the connecting site and object tradition. [Feigenberg, *Nikolai Bernstein: From Reflex to the Model of the Future*](https://dokumen.pub/nikolai-bernstein-from-reflex-to-the-model-of-the-future.html), [Sirotkina, *Mir kak zhivoe dvizhenie*](https://dokumen.pub/978-5-89353-524-2.html)

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Bernstein met Wiener in Moscow during Wiener’s 1960 Soviet visit. Bernstein and Alexander Luria interpreted Wiener’s lecture; afterward Bernstein personally gave Wiener his 1935 paper “The Problem of the Interrelation of Coordination and Localization,” which developed ideas about circular regulation and feedback in movement control. The evidence supports the meeting and exchange, but not later legends that Wiener formally conceded wholesale priority for cybernetics to Bernstein. [Sirotkina, *Mir kak zhivoe dvizhenie*](https://dokumen.pub/978-5-89353-524-2.html)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Bernstein engaged Wiener’s published cybernetic work in his later writings, adopting Wiener’s definition of cybernetics while distinguishing machine goal-direction from the internally generated, anticipatory activity of organisms. This was a substantive written engagement, not merely a retrospective comparison imposed by later scholars. [Feigenberg, *Nikolai Bernstein: From Reflex to the Model of the Future*](https://dokumen.pub/nikolai-bernstein-from-reflex-to-the-model-of-the-future.html), [Sirotkina, *Mir kak zhivoe dvizhenie*](https://dokumen.pub/978-5-89353-524-2.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen interpreted Abraham extensively in his *Commentary* and *Homilies on Genesis*, begun at Alexandria and continued during his Caesarean career (c. 220s–240s); he also defended Abraham’s ancestral and religious significance in *Against Celsus* 4.33–35 (c. 248, Caesarea). [Origen, *Against Celsus* 4](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04164.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen repeatedly treated Aaron’s priesthood, vestments, sacrifices, and relationship to Moses in his Caesarean *Homilies on Exodus*, *Leviticus*, and *Numbers*, generally interpreting Aaronic institutions typologically in relation to Christ and the Church. The connection is textual, not historical contact.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen devoted his second *Homily on Genesis* to Noah’s ark and returned to Noah in his homilies on Ezekiel, where he interpreted Ezekiel’s triad of Noah, Daniel, and Job. These sermons belong to his third-century exegetical ministry, principally associated with Caesarea. [Origen, *Homilies on Genesis and Exodus*](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5d7fd6172ce70f2732bc7dd0/t/65e8a0d73614cf0867d8fac2/1709744343774/Origen%2B-%2BGenesis%2BHomily%2BII.pdf) [Origen, *Homilies on Ezekiel*](https://www.roger-pearse.com/weblog/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/Origen-Homilies_on_Ezekiel-ed_Hooker-2014.pdf)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Moses was a major subject throughout Origen’s commentaries and homilies on the Pentateuch and in *Against Celsus*. Origen defended Moses as legislator and theologian against Celsus while interpreting Mosaic law spiritually for Christians; this work spans Alexandria and Caesarea, c. 220s–248. [Origen, *Against Celsus* 1](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04161.htm) [Origen, *Against Celsus* 3](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04163.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen wrote commentaries, scholia, and numerous homilies on the Psalms attributed to David, from his Alexandrian period through his final Caesarean years. The twenty-nine Greek Psalm homilies recovered in Munich Cod. graec. 314 materially document this engagement. [Eusebius on Origen’s scriptural works](https://www.clarehall.cam.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Eusebius_selected.pdf) [CUA Press, *Homilies on the Psalms*](https://www.cuapress.org/9780813233192/homilies-on-the-psalms/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen treated Solomon as the scriptural authorial persona behind Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. His early and mature commentaries and homilies on the Song—completed after work at Athens, probably in the 240s—made Solomon’s poetry a principal vehicle for ecclesial and mystical interpretation. [Eusebius on Origen’s scriptural works](https://www.clarehall.cam.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Eusebius_selected.pdf)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen composed a large *Commentary on Ezekiel* and preached surviving *Homilies on Ezekiel*. He worked on the commentary at Athens and Caesarea in the late 230s or 240s, interpreting Ezekiel historically, morally, and Christologically. [Origen, *Homilies on Ezekiel*](https://www.roger-pearse.com/weblog/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/Origen-Homilies_on_Ezekiel-ed_Hooker-2014.pdf)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Jesus is the central subject of Origen’s *Commentaries on John* and *Matthew*, his homilies on Luke, *On First Principles*, and *Against Celsus*. Across Alexandria and Caesarea, c. 218–249, Origen wrote about Jesus’s historical ministry, eternal identity as Logos, incarnation, teaching, death, and resurrection. [Origen, *Commentary on Matthew* 12](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/101612.htm) [Origen, *Against Celsus*](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0416.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen wrote a fifteen-book *Commentary on Romans*, commentaries on several other Pauline epistles, and repeatedly interpreted Paul in *On First Principles* and *Against Celsus*. His engagement with Paul extended from the Alexandrian period into his Caesarean teaching and preaching. [Origen, *Against Celsus* 3](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04163.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen repeatedly quoted, compared, and criticized Plato, most explicitly in *Against Celsus* (c. 248). He acknowledged points of agreement—including incorporeal theology—while arguing that biblical revelation surpassed Platonic teaching. [Origen, *Against Celsus* 7.42–43](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04167.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen explicitly discussed Aristotle as Plato’s dissident pupil and founder of a separate philosophical school in *Against Celsus* 3.12–13. Aristotle and Peripatetic reasoning also formed part of the philosophical environment Origen examined for Christian students. [Origen, *Against Celsus* 3](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04163.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen discussed Homer’s poetry and theology in *Against Celsus*, contrasting Homeric stories of divine violence and sexual misconduct with Mosaic teaching and invoking Plato’s exclusion of Homer from the ideal city. This was written at Caesarea around 248. [Origen, *Against Celsus* 4.36](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04164.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** In *Against Celsus* 4.36, Origen named Hesiod alongside Homer and criticized the Greek theogonies for attributing generation and morally scandalous conduct to the gods. [Origen, *Against Celsus* 4](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04164.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen addressed Zoroaster in *Against Celsus* 1.16 while reproducing and contesting Celsus’s catalogue of ancient sages. The notice documents written engagement but does not show access to authentic Zoroastrian writings. [Origen, *Against Celsus* 1](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04161.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Origen cited Josephus by name and recommended his two books *On the Antiquity of the Jews*—now called *Against Apion*—as evidence for Jewish antiquity in *Against Celsus* 1.16. Elsewhere he cited Josephus concerning John the Baptist, James, and Jerusalem’s destruction, although the exact textual history of some passages is disputed. [Origen, *Against Celsus* 1](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04161.htm)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Augustine wrote critically about doctrines attributed to Origen. In correspondence with Jerome around 397 he requested a clearer account of Origen’s condemned errors; in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* (417) he associated Origen with the proposition that postmortem punishment might end. [Augustine, Letter 40](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102040.htm) [Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1505.htm)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Aquinas incorporated numerous passages explicitly attributed to Origen into the *Catena Aurea*, his Gospel commentary compiled c. 1262–1268. The work places Origen’s interpretations in a continuous patristic chain, including substantial excerpts from the commentaries on Matthew and John. [Aquinas, *Catena Aurea* on Matthew](https://ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xvi.html) [Aquinas, *Catena Aurea* on John](https://www.fisheaters.com/srpdf/xaquinas-john.pdf)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Emperor Justinian wrote or promulgated a lengthy theological edict addressed to Patriarch Mennas in 543, summarizing and refuting propositions attributed to Origen and appending anti-Origenist anathemas. The document is a direct posthumous written engagement, although some condemned propositions more accurately represent later Origenism than securely recoverable teachings of Origen himself. [Justinian’s edict and anathemas](https://www.ldysinger.com/%40magist/0543-53_an-orig/03_anath_543-53.htm) [Richard Price, *Acts of Constantinople II*, anti-Origenist documents](https://afkimel.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/the-acts-of-the-council-of-constantinople-of-553-2-vol-edited-and-translated-by-richard-price-translated-texts-for-historians-volume-51-2009-9781846311789-da31e1d5d5690161fc03aafa9daef89.pdf)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact.** Le Plongeon cited “Origenes” in *Sacred Mysteries* (1886) for an account of Mithraic priests imitating the movements of celestial bodies and assuming the names and dress of constellations. [Primary text](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/57458/57458-h/57458-h.htm)

- **[T1+]** In the third century, Origen wrote that Peter preached to the circumcised and was crucified head downward at Rome; the relevant passage from his lost commentary is transmitted by Eusebius in *Church History* 3.1. Peter is the earlier, written-about figure. The textual transmission is a **documented fact**; the head-downward crucifixion itself remains a **reported fact** based on late tradition. [Eusebius, *Church History* 3](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/250103.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Vigenère cited Origen for the proposition that sacred or operative names lose their original force when translated into another language, using it in his concluding discussion of languages and alphabets. [Primary-text transcription, fol. 341v](https://wulfric.artsci.utoronto.ca/rentexte/vigenere/chif_traite.htm)

Origen later discussed Josephus as a non-Christian witness concerning John the Baptist, James, and Jesus.

- **[T1+]** Origen wrote about the earlier Simon in *Against Celsus* during the 240s CE, treating him as a failed divine claimant and reporting that Simonian communities had nearly disappeared. The written engagement is **documented fact**; Origen’s historical and demographic assertions are **reported fact**. [*Against Celsus* 6](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04166.htm)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Wilde discussed Aristotle at length in *The Rise of Historical Criticism*, written at Oxford in 1879, crediting him with establishing an inductive and scientific approach to history and political development. Aristotle is the earlier, written-about figure; Wilde is the later writer. [University College Cork text](https://celt.ucc.ie/published/E800003-001/text001.html)

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Wilde and Arthur Conan Doyle met at J. M. Stoddart’s dinner at London’s Langham Hotel on 30 August 1889. Both accepted commissions for *Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine*, producing *The Picture of Dorian Gray* and *The Sign of the Four*. Doyle’s contemporary pocket diary records the commission, and his autobiography remembers Wilde’s conversation warmly. [Arthur Conan Doyle Collection](https://www.conandoylecollection.com/conan-doyle/you-dont-know-sherlock-holmes-yet/conan-doyles-writings/conan-doyle-and-oscar-wilde), [1889 diary evidence](https://www.arthur-conan-doyle.com/wiki/Conan_Doyle%27s_Pocket_Diary_for_1889)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Dante recurs throughout Wilde’s writing, from the Italian historical setting and Dantean associations of *Ravenna* (1878) to the sustained engagement with Dante, exile, suffering, and the *Divine Comedy* in the prison letter later titled *De Profundis*. Wilde read Dante during his imprisonment and treated him as a principal predecessor in transforming suffering into art. Because Dante is the earlier figure and Wilde wrote about him, Wilde bears the negative sign. [1915 English text of *De Profundis*](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/De_Profundis_%28Wilde%2C_1915%29/De_Profundis)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Around 1876 Wilde wrote the unfinished, approximately 8,500-word essay now called “The Women of Homer,” reviewing John Addington Symonds’s treatment of Homeric women while offering Wilde’s own account of the heroines of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*. The autograph manuscript survives at the Morgan Library. [Morgan Library manuscript record](https://www.themorgan.org/literary-historical/120334), [Oscar Wilde Society publication history](https://oscarwildesociety.co.uk/publications/other-publications/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Wilde made Jesus the subject of an extended literary and religious interpretation in the 1897 prison letter later titled *De Profundis*. He characterized Christ as an intensely imaginative individualist and artist who made himself the voice and image of suffering. This is a documented textual engagement, not evidence that every theological claim in the letter was intended as orthodox doctrine. [Text of *De Profundis*](https://americanliterature.com/author/oscar-wilde/letter/de-profundis)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Wilde attended Ruskin’s Oxford lectures, responded to his teaching through the Hinksey road-building project, and continued corresponding with him after university. Archival catalogues identify surviving letters from Wilde to Ruskin through 1884.
- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Their relationship was personal as well as intellectual: Wilde worked under Ruskin’s direction at Oxford and remained in sufficiently direct contact for Ruskin later to call him a “most true friend.” The precise extent of their later friendship is less fully documented than their Oxford association. [NYPL Ruskin papers](https://archives.nypl.org/brg/19183), [Ruskin research account](https://wp.lancs.ac.uk/the-ruskin/2019/03/14/john-ruskin-the-wildes-and-imaginations-reign/)

Later picturesque stories about their introduction—especially Wilde carpeting her path with flowers—are reported anecdotes rather than securely contemporary documentation. This supports a personal meeting, although the surviving account was published retrospectively and should not be treated as a contemporaneous record of their conversation. [Sherard, *The Real Oscar Wilde*](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/94/The_real_Oscar_Wilde._With_numerous_unpublished_letters%2C_facsims%2C_ports._and_illus_%28IA_cu31924013572205%29.pdf)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Yeats attended Wilde’s Dublin lecture on “The House Beautiful” in November 1883, making this a direct performer-audience crossing under the project’s discourse category. - **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Wilde repeatedly engaged in print with Morris’s work. He reviewed Morris’s translation of the *Odyssey* in the *Pall Mall Gazette* on 24 November 1888 and reported on Morris’s Arts and Crafts lecture about carpet and tapestry weaving. - **[T5]** **Reported fact:** Twain’s reconstructed day-by-day chronology, drawing on his notebooks and documentary record, places a meeting between Twain and Wilde at Bad Nauheim, Germany, in July or August 1892. The available source does not establish a close relationship or a precise day, so the crossing should be recorded only as a reported personal meeting. - **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Wilde treated Plato as a major figure in the development of historical and philosophical criticism in *The Rise of Historical Criticism* and repeatedly engaged Platonic dialogue, aesthetics, and the relationship between truth and art in later criticism, especially “The Critic as Artist.” In *De Profundis* he explicitly paired the sayings of Plato and Christ as ideas transferable into art. [University College Cork text](https://celt.ucc.ie/published/E800003-001/text001.html), [text of *De Profundis*](https://americanliterature.com/author/oscar-wilde/letter/de-profundis)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Martí followed Wilde’s 1882 American tour in the press and produced two substantial portraits: a New York chronicle dated 7 January 1882 and the better-known essay published later that year in Caracas and Buenos Aires. This is one-sided written engagement; no personal meeting between Martí and Wilde has been documented. [Scholarly study of the January chronicle](https://irlandeses.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Irlanda-y-Cuba-historias-entretejidas-030120-with-cover.pdf), [publication-history study](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13569325.2019.1654441)
