Because these narratives were recorded roughly seven centuries after Pindar and contain conventional poet-legend motifs, they document Aelian’s treatment of Pindar but not necessarily the narrated events. **Evidentiary label: documented fact that Aelian wrote about Pindar; rumor or myth for the infancy story and reported fact of uncertain reliability for the competition tradition.** [Aelian, *Various History* 12.45](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/oddnotes/variahistoria/chap1245.html); [Aelian, *Various History* 13.25](https://atlas.perseus.tufts.edu/library/passage/urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0007.tlg088.perseus-eng3:intro-4/)

- **[T3]** Around 197 CE, Tertullian explicitly invokes Pindar in the *Apologeticum*, referring to *Pythian* 3 and its account of Asclepius being struck by lightning after accepting payment connected with his healing art. Tertullian adapts the pagan poem for Christian polemic; the relationship is purely textual. **Evidentiary label: documented fact.** [Tertullian, *Apologeticum* 14](https://st-takla.org/books/en/ecf/003/0030020.html)
Solinus recounted a legend about Pindar’s miraculous rescue and placed him among musicians patronized by Alexander I of Macedon.
Plato quoted or adapted the earlier poet Pindar in discussions of the soul, punishment, and the afterlife.
Simonides and Pindar belonged to the overlapping circle of poets patronized by Hieron I in Syracuse during the 470s BCE.
Cicero cited or discussed Pindar as part of his documented engagement with Greek authors and figures.
Aristotle quoted and discussed the earlier Pindar in rhetorical, ethical, and poetic contexts.

- **[T3]** Pindar’s early-fifth-century-BCE victory odes engage identifiable Hesiodic formulations and narratives. Pythian 6 and Isthmian 6 adapt precepts associated with *Works and Days*, while other odes reshape Hesiodic divine genealogy and cosmic ordering. **Documented fact:** textual reception and transformation, not evidence that Pindar possessed Hesiod’s autograph or met him. [Oxford Handbook discussion](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/27942/chapter-abstract/211866716) [Scholarly review](https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2018/2018.12.12/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Quintilian evaluates Pindar in *Institutio* 10.1.61 as the foremost Greek lyric poet, praising his magnificence, figures, linguistic abundance, and powerful flow while adopting the earlier judgment that his style was inimitable. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html)
Nietzsche repeatedly transformed Pindar's phrase 'become who you are' into a central formula of self-formation.

counterpart_name: María Estela Martínez Cartas de Perón
text: Facio Hebequer introduced Quinquela Martín to Collivadino around 1917, after which Collivadino supported Quinquela materially and professionally and remained part of his social network.
Collivadino and Luis Perlotti participated together in the group that welcomed Quinquela Martín back from Paris and travelled by launch toward La Boca.
Collivadino and Pedro Subercaseaux competed in the same historical-painting contest at the 1910 Buenos Aires Centenary Exhibition.
Collivadino belonged to the institutional lineage of the Buenos Aires art academy in which Ángel della Valle had earlier served as a principal teacher, although no personal contact is documented.
Collivadino later joined the jury that voided the Monument to the Flag competition in which Gianotti had received first prize.
Collivadino belonged to the next Argentine artistic generation and later led institutions descended from the art-education system in which Della Valle taught.
Collivadino taught Perlotti at the Academy of Fine Arts in Buenos Aires, principally from 1909 to 1915.
Collivadino and Christophersen participated in overlapping Argentine artistic institutions during the Salón Nacional era.
Piri wrote about Columbus’s voyage and said that American geography on his 1513 map derived from a chart of Columbus and testimony from a captive who had sailed with him.
Piri included a Saint Brendan-type maritime legend on his 1513 map, probably copied from a medieval European map.
Piri referred to maps purportedly dating from Alexander the Great’s time, invoking Alexander as a conventional marker of geographical antiquity.
Pizarro met Atahualpa at Cajamarca, captured and detained him during the ransom proceedings, and authorized his execution.

counterpart_name: El Inca Garcilaso de la Vega
text: Garcilaso later wrote about Pizarro and the conquest in his historical works.
Guamán Poma later depicted and discussed Pizarro and the conquest in his chronicle.
Valera wrote about Inca history and the conquest after Pizarro's death.
Orellana operated within the expanding Pizarro network through Gonzalo Pizarro's eastern expedition, which was commissioned during Francisco Pizarro's government.
Cortés and Pizarro were both in the orbit of Charles V’s court in the late 1520s, although no personal meeting was securely documented.
Tschiffely wrote about Pizarro and the Spanish conquest of Peru in Coricancha.
Pizarro later participated in the Caribbean and mainland expansion conducted through institutions and routes established after Columbus's voyages.
José González Castillo worked for Glücksmann, wrote lyrics for a prize-winning competition entry, and helped direct Gardel and Razzano to his attention.
A Government Palace space and its imagery were later changed from honoring Pizarro to honoring Túpac Amaru, creating a posthumous symbolic pairing.

- **[T9+]** **Reported fact:** Atahualpa’s gold ceremonial seat or stool became part of the Cajamarca booty and was assigned to Pizarro after the ransom was melted and divided in June 1533. Pedro Sancho’s proximate relation describes an exceptionally valuable gold seat among the objects brought from Cuzco; other colonial accounts explicitly identify the object allotted to Pizarro as the seat on which Atahualpa had been carried or seated. [Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes](https://www.cervantesvirtual.com/obra-visor/cronistas-coloniales-primera-parte--0/html/0000fb16-82b2-11df-acc7-002185ce6064_8.html), [Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes](https://www.cervantesvirtual.com/obra-visor/historia-de-la-vida-y-hechos-del-emperador-carlos-v--2/html/feecfcca-82b1-11df-acc7-002185ce6064_27.htm)
Spence wrote critically about Pizarro and the conquest of Peru in his historical introduction to Inca religion and mythology.
Aristotle studied in Plato’s Academy for roughly twenty years, reported Plato’s doctrines, and criticized several parts of his philosophy.
Diogenes probably lived in Athens during Plato’s later years, although the anecdotes describing conversations between them are unverified.
Plato repeatedly quoted, analyzed, praised, and criticized the earlier poet Homer.
Plato quoted and criticized Hesiod’s theology and philosophically reworked material from his myths.
Plato quoted or adapted the earlier poet Pindar in discussions of the soul, punishment, and the afterlife.
Plato is understood to have engaged with themes found in the earlier Herodotus, including ethnography, constitutions, Egypt, and empire.
A planetary device associated with the later Archimedes was linked by Cicero to the cosmological tradition of Plato’s Timaeus.
Plato and Alexander were indirectly connected through Aristotle and Plato’s Academy, although they did not meet.
The later Cicero translated part of Plato’s Timaeus, imitated Platonic dialogue, and explicitly engaged Plato in his political works.
The later Augustine received Plato indirectly through Latin Neoplatonic books that directed him toward immaterial reality.
The later Origen engaged Platonic questions about incorporeal reality, the soul, and intelligible order within Christian theology.
The later Tertullian engaged and attacked Platonic elements in Christian philosophical speculation.
The later Maimonides encountered transformed Platonism indirectly through Arabic philosophical traditions.

counterpart_name: Abu Yusuf Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi
text: The later al-Kindi received Platonic and Neoplatonic material through Arabic translation, paraphrase, and late-antique synthesis.
Albertus Magnus encountered Plato’s doctrines indirectly through Christian, Arabic, Aristotelian, and commentarial traditions.
Thomas Aquinas encountered Plato’s doctrines indirectly through Christian, Arabic, Aristotelian, and commentarial traditions.
The later Dante reworked Platonic and Neoplatonic cosmological, ethical, and theological material through Latin Christian traditions.
The later Pico sought to reconcile Plato with Aristotle, Christianity, Kabbalah, and other traditions.
The later Bruno engaged Platonic and Neoplatonic traditions while departing from Plato’s finite cosmology.
The later Galileo participated in a mathematical philosophy of nature interpreted as Platonic, though simple direct descent is uncertain.
The later Kepler explicitly used Platonic solids and Timaeus-like mathematical cosmology in his astronomical work.
The later Descartes developed ideas with Platonic analogues, although direct borrowing from Plato remains uncertain.
The later Leibniz read and discussed Plato and interpreted Platonic commitments through early modern rationalism.
The later Kant discussed Plato’s Ideas while distinguishing his transcendental account from dogmatic uses of Platonic Forms.
The later Hegel lectured extensively on Plato and interpreted the dialogues within his history of philosophy.
The later Nietzsche repeatedly treated Plato as a major philosophical opponent while recognizing his artistic and political power.
The later Kierkegaard engaged Plato as a principal source on Socrates while questioning Plato’s historical reliability.
The later Heidegger repeatedly interpreted Plato’s cave allegory and account of truth as decisive for Western metaphysics.
The later Foucault analyzed Platonic treatments of truth-telling, self-care, politics, and philosophical life.
The later Derrida analyzed Plato’s Phaedrus in relation to writing, memory, and the pharmakon.
The later Deleuze framed part of his philosophical project as reversing Plato’s hierarchy of models, copies, and simulacra.
The later Habermas placed Platonic dialogue and rational argument within the historical predevelopment of philosophical discourse.
The later Žižek frequently invoked Plato’s politics, universality, and communism in his own work.
The Ghāya invoked Plato as an earlier textual authority, often through pseudonymous or late antique Arabic works.
Wiener traced the word cybernetics to the vocabulary of steering and governance found in Plato.
Later anecdotes portray Diogenes and Plato as personal and intellectual rivals, although their actual contact is uncertain.
Austin studied Plato and left notes on the Republic that were later reconstructed for publication.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact; underlying use: theory.** Plato was a major ancient authority in Le Plongeon’s published system. In *Sacred Mysteries* (1886) and *Queen Móo and the Egyptian Sphinx* (1896), Le Plongeon treated Plato’s Atlantis account as substantially historical and claimed that Maya records independently confirmed it. [1886 primary text](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/57458/57458-h/57458-h.htm), [1896 primary text](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/03/Queen_M%C3%B3o_and_the_Egyptian_sphinx_-_by_Augustus_Le_Plongeon_%28IA_cu31924083722037%29.pdf)
Roger Bacon engaged Plato indirectly through Latin traditions and authorities that influenced the organization of his later philosophy.
Dick's philosophical and theological writings engaged the earlier philosopher Plato's ideas about appearance, reality, and forms.
More engaged and reworked Plato's political philosophy, especially the Republic, throughout Utopia.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Wells wrote about Plato and the Academy in *The Outline of History* and engaged directly with Platonic political philosophy in *A Modern Utopia*. Plato supplied both a precedent for utopian social construction and a model against which Wells defined his own modern, evolutionary utopia. [Wells works index and *Outline* contents](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/57490/57490-h/57490-h.htm)
A possibly pseudo-Platonic text referred to Zoroaster in connection with Persian royal religious instruction.
Solinus recounted the ceremonial reception that the Syracusan ruler Dionysius reportedly gave Plato.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Plato is a major recurring authority in Vigenère’s symbolic cosmology. The *Traicté des chiffres* invokes Platonic accounts of intelligible light, the formation of humanity, non-being, number, and the construction of the world in the *Timaeus*. [Primary-text transcription, dedication and fols. 19v and 139v](https://wulfric.artsci.utoronto.ca/rentexte/vigenere/chif_traite.htm)

counterpart_name: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
text: Sor Juana’s poetry and philosophy engaged indirectly with the broader Neoplatonic tradition transmitted through later Christian and Renaissance writers.

- **[T3]** Plato repeatedly engages Pindar’s poetry, quoting or naming him in works including the *Gorgias* (484b, the “law is king” fragment), *Meno* (81b–c, verses concerning Persephone and the soul), *Republic*, and *Laws* 3.690b–c. These are direct fourth-century-BCE textual engagements with Pindar’s words and authority, not evidence of a personal relationship. **Evidentiary label: documented fact.** [Plato, *Gorgias* 484b](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Plat.%20Gorg.%20484b); [Plato, *Meno* 81b–c](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Plat.%20Meno%2081b); [Plato, *Laws* 3](https://classics.mit.edu/Plato/laws.3.iii.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Lorenzo explicitly invoked and praised Plato in the philosophical poem *De summo bono*, now generally called the *Altercazione*, written in the 1470s. The poem calls him “divine Plato” while treating the nature of the highest good; its Platonism was mediated substantially through Marsilio Ficino. [Text of the *Altercazione*](https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/Opere_%28Lorenzo_de%27_Medici%29/X._Altercazione/Capitolo_I.), [Treccani on Lorenzo’s Ficinian works](https://www.treccani.it/magazine/strumenti/una_poesia_al_giorno/07_22_Medici_Lorenzo_de.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Wilde treated Plato as a major figure in the development of historical and philosophical criticism in *The Rise of Historical Criticism* and repeatedly engaged Platonic dialogue, aesthetics, and the relationship between truth and art in later criticism, especially “The Critic as Artist.” In *De Profundis* he explicitly paired the sayings of Plato and Christ as ideas transferable into art. [University College Cork text](https://celt.ucc.ie/published/E800003-001/text001.html), [text of *De Profundis*](https://americanliterature.com/author/oscar-wilde/letter/de-profundis)
Virgil’s mature poetry engages with Platonic themes, although the extent and directness of that engagement are disputed.
The corpus associated with Ahmad al-Majriti presents Plato as an ancient magical and philosophical authority through largely pseudepigraphic or late-antique traditions.
Schelling drew on Plato’s forms and dialogue method in Bruno and his philosophy of ideas.
Dugin repeatedly wrote about Plato and Platonism, directly engaging Platonic dialogues and incorporating Platonic thought into his account of the Apollonian Logos.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Agrippa repeatedly interpreted Plato and Platonic cosmology. Ficino’s translations and commentaries supplied much of his access to Plato, and Agrippa lectured or wrote on the *Symposium*. Platonic doctrines of the world soul, cosmic hierarchy, love, and intellectual ascent became structural components of *De occulta philosophia*. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/agrippa-nettesheim/)
Plato repeatedly discussed Simonides and interpreted works and sayings attributed to him in the Protagoras and Republic.
Pitois portrayed Plato as a student of Egyptian priests or Magi and presented Platonism as descending from Egyptian initiatory wisdom.
Reuchlin repeatedly discussed and quoted Plato in his synthesis of philosophy and Christian Kabbalah.
Josephus compared Plato's ideal legislation with the Mosaic constitution and polemically alleged that Plato followed principles resembling Jewish law.

counterpart_name: Abu Yusuf Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi
text: Al-Kindī engaged with Platonic material, often through indirect or abridged textual sources.
Camillo adapted Platonic Ideas as eternal places within the Theatre’s supersensible order.
Searle discussed this earlier philosopher's ideas while addressing theories of mind, action, perception, reason, language, or social reality.
Vico read Plato intensively and identified him as the first of his four principal authors.
Plato used Odyssean scenes and quotations, including Odysseus’s soul choosing a private life in the Republic.
Lacan used Plato's Symposium extensively in Seminar VIII.
Schumpeter discussed Plato's treatment of the division of labor, the ideal state, and the relationship between economics and political philosophy.
Plato later analyzed Cyrus’s education, government, family policy, and succession in Laws III.
Newton wrote a notebook motto invoking Plato and used Platonic and Neoplatonic materials in his studies of ancient philosophy.
Blavatsky used Platonic and Neoplatonic metaphysics as central sources for Isis Unveiled and her account of perennial wisdom.
Scholars have reconstructed Platonic themes in Vanini’s lost De contemnenda gloria, though their precise extent cannot be verified.
Rousseau used Plato's Republic as a central precedent for treating education as political formation.
Nizami incorporated Plato as one of the Greek sages in the philosophical world of the Eskandar-nama.

- **[T1-]** Aelian made Plato (died 348/347 BCE) a recurring subject of *Varia historia*, relating anecdotes about his habits, humility, pupils, travels, philosophical rivalries, and reception. These are retrospective literary notices written approximately five and a half centuries later. **Documented fact** that Aelian wrote about Plato; the historicity of individual anecdotes is variable ([*Varia historia* 2.18](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist2.html), [3.17](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist3.html), [4.9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aelian/varhist4.html)).
Balfour discussed Plato as an earlier philosopher in Theism and Humanism.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Schrödinger discussed Plato as part of his historical examination of Greek natural philosophy, the conflict between reason and sensory evidence, and the intellectual ancestry of modern science in lectures delivered at University College Dublin in 1948 and published as *Nature and the Greeks* (1954). This is a later author’s engagement with an ancient figure, not evidence for any direct or esoteric transmission. See the [Cambridge University Press edition](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/nature-and-the-greeks-and-science-and-humanism/9781107431836).
Campanella drew on and modified political and social ideas from Plato’s Republic when composing The City of the Sun.
Satie drew on Plato as a past author by setting French translations of Platonic passages in Socrate.
Yates analyzed Platonic recollection and the Phaedrus in The Art of Memory.
Dewey discussed Plato's educational and political philosophy extensively in Democracy and Education.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Quintilian discusses Plato as both philosopher and prose stylist, recommends him among the foremost philosophical authors for an orator, and compares the copious flow of Plato’s writing with qualities realized in Cicero. The connection is sustained textual engagement with a predecessor who died more than three centuries before Quintilian’s birth. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html)
Copernicus discussed Plato’s arrangement of Mercury and Venus and invoked him when commenting on ancient astronomers.
Pike frequently invoked Plato while discussing metaphysics, the Good, the soul, initiation, symbolism, and intelligible and material worlds.
Sartre engaged Plato as a persistent reference point inherited through his classical philosophical education.
Borges repeatedly used Platonic forms and the nominalism-realism dispute as literary material.
Nicholas engaged Plato through Latin sources, Proclus, and Byzantine contacts, incorporating Platonizing ideas into his writings.
Goethe read and reworked the intellectual tradition associated with this earlier figure without any historical meeting.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Alberti cited and discussed Plato in *De re aedificatoria* and elsewhere, drawing upon Platonic political, cosmological, and aesthetic arguments while incorporating them into an eclectic rather than doctrinally Platonist philosophy. Landino later made Alberti a principal Platonic speaker in the *Disputationes Camaldulenses*, but the specific doctrines placed in his mouth there are a **reported fact/literary representation**, not secure evidence of Alberti’s exact spoken words.
Spence repeatedly interpreted Plato's writings on Atlantis and also discussed his conception of the afterlife.

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** Polybius explicitly engages Plato’s political thought. In *Histories* 6 he compares his account of constitutional transformation with Plato’s more elaborate treatment, while in Book 12 he adapts Plato’s proposition about philosophers and kings to argue that history improves when experienced statesmen write it or historians acquire practical experience. [Polybius, *Histories* 6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/6%2A.html), [*Histories* 12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/12%2A.html)

counterpart_name: Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci
text: Leonardo engaged with a Pythagorean-Platonic intellectual tradition, often through Renaissance intermediaries, although his direct reading of Plato is uncertain.
Pliny used Aristotle as a named authority in discussions of zoology, biology, cosmology, and nature.
Pliny wrote about Archimedes as a mathematical and mechanical authority and repeated traditions concerning his achievements and death.
Pliny wrote about Alexander in accounts of exploration, artistic patronage, precious materials, and territories opened to Macedonian inquiry.
Pliny used and sometimes criticized Ctesias as a source on eastern geography, animals, and marvelous peoples.
Pliny cited or discussed Caesar in the Natural History.
The later writer Solinus drew extensively on Pliny's Natural History for geography and accounts of marvels.
Pliny named Herodotus as a source for geography, ethnography, and traditions about marvels.
Pliny repeatedly discussed Homer as a source for geography, natural lore, and early cultural traditions.
Pliny cited Cicero and received rhetorical, linguistic, and philosophical material from his writings.
Pliny used and sometimes corrected Virgil as an authority on agriculture, plants, bees, and Italian geography.
Pliny wrote about Zoroaster as the inventor of magic and repeated traditions concerning his infancy and attributed writings.
Solinus extensively excerpted, compressed, rearranged, and sometimes corrected material from Pliny’s Natural History.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Vigenère cited Pliny on ancient finger-numbering, metallurgy, geography, and historical examples, including the finger positions of a statue of Janus and the crucifixion of Polycrates. [Primary-text transcription, fols. 14r and 292r](https://wulfric.artsci.utoronto.ca/rentexte/vigenere/chif_traite.htm)

- **[T3]** Pliny records Pindar-related historical tradition in *Natural History* 7, particularly the claim that Alexander spared Pindar’s house and descendants during the destruction of Thebes. Pliny wrote in the first century CE and supplies reception testimony rather than eyewitness evidence about Pindar. **Evidentiary label: documented fact that Pliny reported the story; reported fact as to the underlying event.** [Pliny, *Natural History* 7](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0137%3Abook%3D7)
Paul made substantial one-sided textual use of Pliny’s Natural History in the geography and antiquarian material of Historia Langobardorum.
Pliny the Elder preserved and engaged with Virgil-related agricultural and natural-historical material.

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Pliny the Elder named and used Megasthenes throughout the *Natural History* (completed in the first century CE), transmitting his geographical, ethnographic, and zoological claims—for example, enormous Indian serpents and extraordinary peoples. Pliny therefore became a major later conduit for Megasthenes’ lost work. [Pliny, *Natural History* 6](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0137%3Abook%3D6&force=y), [8.14](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0137%3Abook%3D8%3Achapter%3D14)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact (later literary report):** In *Natural History* 9.119–121, completed about 77 CE, Pliny made Cleopatra the protagonist of the famous pearl-banquet story, claiming that she dissolved and drank an extraordinarily valuable pearl during a wager with Antony. Pliny unquestionably wrote the account, but the incident itself is an uncorroborated luxury exemplum composed roughly a century after the alleged event. [Pliny, *Natural History* IX](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0137%3Abook%3D9&force=y)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Agrippa encountered Pliny’s *Natural History* during his Cologne education and later mined it for reports about stones, plants, animals, medicines, sympathies, and antipathies. Pliny was therefore a major written-about and excerpted ancient authority in Agrippa’s natural magic. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/agrippa-nettesheim/)
Pliny credited Simonides with inventing technical memory, documenting the poet’s Roman-era reputation as a mnemonic innovator.
Columbus owned and annotated an Italian edition of Pliny's Natural History and drew geographical and natural-historical material from it.
Pliny incorporated and sometimes explicitly attributed Ctesian material concerning unusual Indian peoples and longevity in his Natural History.
Kircher worked within a natural-historical textual tradition in which Plinio el Viejo was a recurring ancient authority.
Pliny the Elder incorporated Aristotelian zoological and natural-historical material into the Natural History, directly or through intermediaries.
Pliny the Elder later wrote about Pytheas by explicitly attributing reports concerning Thule, Abalus, amber, and northern peoples to him.

- **[T1+]** Pliny explicitly discusses Hesiod in the first century CE. *Natural History* 14.3 presents him as an early transmitter of agricultural rules, while other books cite Hesiodic botanical, astronomical, and mythographic material. **Documented fact:** direct later written testimony and source use; Pliny’s “thousand years” is rhetorical chronology, and some material he knew as Hesiodic may have belonged to the wider attributed corpus. [*Natural History* 14.3](https://www.attalus.org/pliny/hn14a.html)

- **[T3]** Pliny names and mines Herodotus repeatedly in the *Natural History*, treating him as an authority—though not always an unquestioned one—on peoples, animals, plants, geography, and marvels. **Documented fact:** direct first-century CE textual engagement with the *Histories* and its ethnographic-natural-historical material. [Pliny, *Natural History*, index of authors](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Plin.%20Nat.%201)
Pliny later transmitted classical accounts of Babylon and Mesopotamian wonders rather than firsthand knowledge of Nebuchadnezzar.
Paracelsus engaged a natural-historical tradition transmitted through Pliny, although the extent of direct dependence varies by work.
Borges drew upon Pliny's natural-history and wonder traditions in works including El libro de los seres imaginarios.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Albert repeatedly used and evaluated Pliny’s *Natural History* in works including *De animalibus*, *De vegetabilibus*, and *De mineralibus*. He transmitted some Plinian reports but also criticized particular claims when observation or other evidence appeared to contradict them. [Albertus Magnus, *On Animals* bibliographic record](https://albertusmagnus.uwaterloo.ca/), [Science History Institute](https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/albertus-magnus-mineralogy-and-the-secrets-of-women/)

- **[T1+]** **Reported fact.** Writing in the first century CE, Pliny reports that Scipio Aemilianus supplied Polybius with ships for an exploratory voyage along Atlantic Africa and summarizes geographical observations attributed to Polybius beyond Mount Atlas. Because Polybius’s relevant geographical writing is lost, Pliny is an important later witness, although the voyage’s extent remains disputed. [Pliny, *Natural History* 5.9](https://www.attalus.org/pliny/hn5a.html)

counterpart_name: Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci
text: Leonardo’s book lists include Pliny’s Natural History, which he used as a textual source.
Mark Twain invoked Pocahontas in chapter 14 of The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson as part of his satire of Virginia pedigree, racial classification, and invented ancestry.
Salavarrieta and Bolívar belonged to the same wider revolutionary milieu, although no meeting between them is documented.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact.** In *Histories* 8, written in the second century BCE, Polybius assesses Alexander’s conquests and attributes part of their success to the courage and discipline of the associates formed under Philip II. Alexander died at Babylon in 323 BCE, more than a century before Polybius’s birth. [Polybius, *Histories* 8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/8%2A.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact.** Polybius narrates Archimedes’ defense of Syracuse against the Roman forces of Marcellus during the siege of 214–212 BCE, describing the mathematician’s artillery, cranes, and countermeasures against naval assault. Polybius was not an eyewitness; he wrote several decades after Archimedes’ death. [Polybius, *Histories* 8.3–7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/8%2A.html)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** Cicero engaged with Polybius as a historical and constitutional authority in the first century BCE, after Polybius’s death. Most notably, Cicero’s treatment of Rome’s constitution in *De re publica* draws substantially on the Polybian analysis of mixed government; this is literary reception, not evidence that the two men met. [Perseus biographical and reception notice](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.04.0104%3Aentry%3Dpolybius-bio-4)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** In *Jewish Antiquities* 12, composed in the 90s CE, Josephus explicitly invokes “Polybius of Megalopolis” and quotes Book 16 of the *Histories* concerning Ptolemaic general Scopas’s campaign against the Jews, probably in 201/200 BCE. This is direct one-sided textual engagement across more than two centuries. [Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities* 12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/josephus/ant-12.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact.** Polybius made Hannibal a central historical subject, particularly in *Histories* 3, reconstructing the Carthaginian’s 218 BCE passage from Iberia through Gaul and across the Alps and analyzing his command decisions during the Second Punic War. Polybius was born after the Alpine crossing and did not meet Hannibal; his connection is historiographical, based on testimony, documents, and later inspection of the route. [Polybius, *Histories* 3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3%2A.html)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** Polybius engaged with Herodotus’s geographical and ethnographic writing. A surviving fragment of *Histories* 12 explicitly compares Polybius’s own observation of the North African lotus with Herodotus’s account. This is textual engagement with a fifth-century-BCE predecessor, not a personal connection. [Polybius, *Histories* 12.2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/12%2A.html)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** Polybius repeatedly quotes and interprets Homer. Among the surviving examples, *Histories* 12 invokes Homeric passages while discussing historical truth and other historians’ arguments. The famous report of Scipio Aemilianus quoting Homer while Carthage burned in 146 BCE is also transmitted through Polybius, though its precise literary shaping remains uncertain. [Polybius, *Histories* 12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/12%2A.html)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** Polybius explicitly engages Plato’s political thought. In *Histories* 6 he compares his account of constitutional transformation with Plato’s more elaborate treatment, while in Book 12 he adapts Plato’s proposition about philosophers and kings to argue that history improves when experienced statesmen write it or historians acquire practical experience. [Polybius, *Histories* 6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/6%2A.html), [*Histories* 12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/12%2A.html)

- **[T1+]** **Reported fact.** Writing in the first century CE, Pliny reports that Scipio Aemilianus supplied Polybius with ships for an exploratory voyage along Atlantic Africa and summarizes geographical observations attributed to Polybius beyond Mount Atlas. Because Polybius’s relevant geographical writing is lost, Pliny is an important later witness, although the voyage’s extent remains disputed. [Pliny, *Natural History* 5.9](https://www.attalus.org/pliny/hn5a.html)

- **[T1-]** **Reported fact.** In the lost geographical Book 34 of the *Histories*, Polybius attacked the credibility of Pytheas’s fourth-century-BCE northern travels, including his reports about Britain, Thule, and the substance conventionally translated as “sea-lung.” The connection survives chiefly through Strabo’s later quotations and paraphrases, so the existence of Polybius’s polemic is documented while its exact original wording and context are not. [Strabo, *Geography* 2.4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Strabo/2D%2A.html)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** Strabo’s *Geography*, composed in the late first century BCE and early first century CE, repeatedly quotes, paraphrases, and criticizes Polybius’s lost geographical Book 34. Strabo preserves Polybius’s case against Pytheas while also challenging Polybius’s own distances and geographical judgments. The relationship is entirely textual; Strabo was born around the end of Polybius’s life and there is no evidence of a meeting. [Strabo, *Geography* 2.4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Strabo/2D%2A.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Quintilian discusses Aristotle repeatedly as a foundational theorist of rhetoric and, in *Institutio oratoria* 10.1, recommends him among the principal Greek philosophical writers useful to an orator. This is a textual engagement across roughly four centuries, not a personal connection. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Cicero is Quintilian’s dominant Roman predecessor and model. Throughout the *Institutio*, completed at Rome c. 95–96 CE, Quintilian quotes, evaluates, and sometimes disputes Cicero’s rhetorical writings, speeches, political conduct, and mnemonic teaching. In Book 10 he declares Cicero the supreme pattern for students; in Book 11 he reproduces Cicero’s formulation of places and images in artificial memory. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html) [*Institutio oratoria* 11.2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/11B%2A.html)

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Frances A. Yates wrote extensively about Quintilian in *The Art of Memory* (1966), treating *Institutio oratoria* 11.2 as one of the three principal surviving Latin accounts of classical artificial memory and calling it the clearest ancient description of the architectural mnemonic procedure. [Yates, *The Art of Memory*](https://resources.warburg.sas.ac.uk/mnemosyne/fq/yates_memory.pdf) [University of Chicago Press](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/A/bo91674300.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Quintilian writes about Herodotus as a stylistic and historiographical model, pairing him with Livy in *Institutio* 10.1.101 and elsewhere invoking Herodotus’s account of the language experiment involving isolated children. The relationship is exclusively literary and retrospective. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** In his Greek literary canon (*Institutio* 10.1.52), Quintilian evaluates Hesiod’s poetry, criticizing its limited elevation while praising its moral maxims and smooth intermediate style as useful to students of eloquence. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Quintilian gives Homer first place in his recommended Greek canon, analyzing the *Iliad* and *Odyssey* as models of narration, emotional appeal, characterization, proof, refutation, and deliberative and forensic speech. He describes Homer as the source from which every department of eloquence flows. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1.46–51](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Quintilian evaluates Julius Caesar as both writer and orator. In the Roman prose canon he praises Caesar’s force, acuteness, energy, and stylistic elegance and judges that, had Caesar devoted himself principally to advocacy, he could have rivaled Cicero. This is retrospective literary criticism, written more than a century after Caesar’s death. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html)

- **[T3]** **Allegation or theory:** Peter of Ravenna’s *Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria* (Venice, 1491) belongs to the post-recovery mnemonic tradition in which Quintilian’s complete text was available. Frances Yates specifically argues that Peter’s accumulation of memory places during journeys reflects Quintilian, uniquely among the principal classical sources, allowing loci to be formed along journeys. Direct dependence is a scholarly inference rather than Peter’s documented declaration of engagement. [Yates, *The Art of Memory*, pp. 111–13](https://resources.warburg.sas.ac.uk/mnemosyne/fq/yates_memory.pdf)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Quintilian evaluates Pindar in *Institutio* 10.1.61 as the foremost Greek lyric poet, praising his magnificence, figures, linguistic abundance, and powerful flow while adopting the earlier judgment that his style was inimitable. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Quintilian discusses Plato as both philosopher and prose stylist, recommends him among the foremost philosophical authors for an orator, and compares the copious flow of Plato’s writing with qualities realized in Cicero. The connection is sustained textual engagement with a predecessor who died more than three centuries before Quintilian’s birth. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Quintilian writes about Simonides in two distinct contexts: *Institutio* 10.1.64 assesses his lyric style and exceptional ability to excite pity, while 11.2 recounts the collapsed-banquet story attributing discovery of ordered mnemonic places to him. Quintilian reports the latter as a traditional account rather than personal or contemporary evidence; its historical core remains unverified. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html) [*Institutio oratoria* 11.2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/11B%2A.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Quintilian repeatedly quotes and analyzes Virgil and begins his Roman poetic canon with him, judging him the Latin epic poet nearest to Homer. He also preserves Domitius Afer’s answer to Quintilian’s own youthful question about Virgil’s rank, making the assessment part of Quintilian’s remembered Roman education before 59 CE. [*Institutio oratoria* 10.1.85–86](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Quintilian/Institutio_Oratoria/10A%2A.html)

- **[T3]** In *Institutio Oratoria* 10.1.61, composed in the late first century CE, Quintilian ranks Pindar foremost among the nine Greek lyric poets and praises his inspiration, grandeur, figures, verbal abundance, and “flood” of eloquence. This is explicit critical engagement with Pindar’s literary reputation. **Evidentiary label: documented fact.** [Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria* 10.1.61](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Aabo%3Aphi%2C1002%2C001%3A10%3A1%3A61)

text: Beauvoir studied Descartes and later engaged with his treatment of subjectivity.

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Comenius visited Descartes at Endegeest near Leiden in July 1642, and the two discussed their competing conceptions of method and universal knowledge. Comenius later described the encounter in *Continuatio admonitionis fraternae*; Descartes had already produced a written assessment of Comenius’s *Pansophiae prodromus*, and Comenius later published anti-Cartesian arguments. The meeting itself is secure, but the often-repeated claim that their conversation lasted precisely four hours rests principally on later narrative transmission. [Brill, *Comenius and the Low Countries* contents and study](https://brill.com/display/book/9789004618879/front-1.pdf); [study of Descartes’s assessment and Comenius’s account](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0960878042000253060)
Euler examined Descartes in his master’s dissertation and developed mathematics inherited from the Cartesian analytical-geometry tradition.
Chomsky connected linguistic creativity to the rationalist tradition associated with Descartes in Cartesian Linguistics.
Leibniz studied and criticized Descartes's metaphysics, physics, mathematics, and mind-body dualism, including in a 1686 paper disputing his account of conserved quantity.
Breton framed Surrealism in opposition to what he regarded as restrictive Cartesian rationalism.
Hooke critically discussed Descartes’s vortex theory of gravity, arguing that lunar gravity and motion created difficulties for it.
Searle discussed this earlier philosopher's ideas while addressing theories of mind, action, perception, reason, language, or social reality.
Vico engaged Cartesian writings, retained some early Cartesian elements, and later criticized Descartes's geometrical method.
Descartes later wrote that Kepler was his first teacher in optics and more knowledgeable in the field than his predecessors.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** In the historical survey of *Psychologie consonantiste* (1938), Odobleja situated Descartes among earlier mechanistic or physically oriented approaches to psychology. This was retrospective intellectual engagement, not evidence of any direct lineage beyond Odobleja’s discussion of Descartes’s ideas. [Digitized volume and indexed text](https://www.scribd.com/document/472087793/Psychologie-consonantiste-vol-I-1938)
Descartes engaged with Campanella’s De sensu rerum by expressing a dismissive judgment about it.
Maxwell discussed Descartes’s definitions of matter and motion while tracing the background to Newtonian dynamics in Matter and Motion.
Locke read Descartes and later opposed Cartesian doctrines such as innate ideas in the Essay.
Yates examined Descartes in relation to the German Rosicrucian controversy and the transition to Cartesian philosophy.
Fourier published work discussing the use of Descartes’s rule of signs to locate polynomial roots.
Sartre critically transformed Descartes's earlier ideas about consciousness and freedom.
Jacobi delivered a public lecture about Descartes in Berlin in January 1846.
Huygens repeatedly analyzed and criticized Descartes’s collision rules and vortex theory of gravity.
Borges engaged in his essays and fiction with Cartesian dreams, skepticism, and the cogito.
Kierkegaard critically examined Cartesian doubt in Johannes Climacus and later philosophical works.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Girard interpreted Abraham’s interrupted sacrifice of Isaac as a biblical disclosure of the transition away from human sacrifice. The episode appears in *Things Hidden since the Foundation of the World* and later biblical conversations. [St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology](https://www.saet.ac.uk/Christianity/ReneGirardandMimeticTheory)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Girard published “Camus’s Stranger Retried” in *PMLA* in 1964, analyzing the narrative judgment and sacrificial dynamics surrounding Meursault. The essay received the MLA’s William Riley Parker Prize in 1965. [Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://iep.utm.edu/girard/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Girard repeatedly situated his account of mimesis against Aristotle’s treatment of imitation and tragedy, especially in *Violence and the Sacred* and *Things Hidden since the Foundation of the World*. Aristotle was a conceptual predecessor, not a person Girard claimed to have superseded in every respect. [Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://iep.utm.edu/girard/)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Girard engaged extensively and critically with Lévi-Strauss’s books on myth, kinship, structuralism, and sacrifice. Girard called Lévi-Strauss, “without knowing it,” his anthropology teacher, while emphasizing their disagreements; *Violence and the Sacred* includes a sustained section on Lévi-Strauss, structuralism, and marriage rules. This supports one-sided written engagement, not a documented friendship. [Association Recherches Mimétiques bibliography](https://old.rene-girard.fr/57_p_44437/bibliographie.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Girard wrote repeatedly about Nietzsche’s opposition to Christianity, including “Nietzsche versus the Crucified,” “Dionysus versus the Crucified,” and the Nietzsche sections of *I See Satan Fall Like Lightning* and *Battling to the End*. Girard treated Nietzsche as an unusually perceptive witness to Christianity’s defense of victims while rejecting his anti-Christian conclusion. [Association Recherches Mimétiques bibliography](https://old.rene-girard.fr/57_p_44437/bibliographie.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Girard discussed and criticized Hegel’s account of desire, recognition, historical reconciliation, and the end of history, most extensively in *Achever Clausewitz* (2007). He acknowledged the Hegelian intellectual climate surrounding his first book but denied that mimetic theory was simply a derivative of Kojève’s Hegel. [Association Recherches Mimétiques](https://old.rene-girard.fr/offres/gestion/events_57_dd_oui-1/.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** *Mensonge romantique et vérité romanesque* (1961; English, *Deceit, Desire and the Novel*, 1965) reads Flaubert’s *Madame Bovary* as a principal example of mediated desire: Emma learns what to desire through prestigious literary and social models. [Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://iep.utm.edu/girard/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Girard discussed Stravinsky near the conclusion of the filmed 2007 Centre Pompidou conversation *Le Sens de l’histoire*, subsequently presented with *La Conversion de l’art*. The evidence supports intellectual treatment, not personal acquaintance. [Association Recherches Mimétiques](https://old.rene-girard.fr/offres/gestion/events_57_oui-1/evenements-rene-girard-association-recherches-mimetiques.htmlhttp%3A/www.rene-girard.fr/offres/gestion/events_57_oui-1/evenements-rene-girard-association-recherches-mimetiques.html)

- **[T4]** **Documented fact:** Girard and Derrida were present at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore for “The Languages of Criticism and the Sciences of Man,” 18–21 October 1966. Girard was a co-organizer; Derrida delivered “Structure, Sign, and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences.” Their shared conference is documented, but the evidence cited here does not establish friendship or sustained correspondence. [Johns Hopkins University](https://hub.jhu.edu/2018/08/08/rene-girard-evolution-desire/)

- **[T4]** **Documented fact:** Lacan participated in the October 1966 Johns Hopkins conference co-organized by Girard. The event put them in the same institutional setting, but no close personal relationship or sustained exchange should be inferred from conference attendance alone. [Association Recherches Mimétiques biography](https://www.rene-girard.fr/biographie-de-rene-girard)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Girard closely read and published criticism of Sartre during his early American career. He later described Sartre as a formative interest rather than a lasting theoretical master. This is documented one-sided intellectual engagement; no personal meeting is established by the sources cited here. [Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://iep.utm.edu/girard/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Jesus and the Passion are central to Girard’s mature anthropology. In *Things Hidden since the Foundation of the World*, *I See Satan Fall Like Lightning*, and related essays, Girard argued that the Gospels expose the persecuting crowd’s scapegoat mechanism and affirm the victim’s innocence. This is Girard’s theological and anthropological interpretation, not independently verified history of the Passion. [St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology](https://www.saet.ac.uk/Christianity/ReneGirardandMimeticTheory)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Proust was one of Girard’s principal literary witnesses to mimetic desire and “novelistic conversion” in *Deceit, Desire and the Novel*. Girard also edited *Proust: A Collection of Critical Essays* and published further studies contrasting Proust with Freud. [Association Recherches Mimétiques](https://old.rene-girard.fr/offres/gestion/actus_57-1/les-actualites-rene-girard-association-recherches-mimetiques.html)

- **[T4]** **Reported fact:** Benoît Chantre’s archival biography describes Girard as an American intermediary for Foucault and other French thinkers and places both men within the network surrounding the 1966 Johns Hopkins conference. Foucault did not deliver one of the conference’s canonical published presentations, so this evidence supports shared milieu more securely than a personal meeting or correspondence. [Association Recherches Mimétiques biography](https://www.rene-girard.fr/biographie-de-rene-girard)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Cervantes’s *Don Quixote* supplies the opening paradigm of triangular desire in *Deceit, Desire and the Novel*: Don Quixote desires through the model of Amadís of Gaul. Girard treated Cervantes as one of the novelists who reveal that supposedly autonomous desire is mediated by another. [Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://iep.utm.edu/girard/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Girard repeatedly analyzed Peter’s denial of Jesus as an example of mimetic contagion and surrender to collective pressure. The Académie française later assigned Girard the dictionary word *reniement*, explicitly resonant with Peter’s denial. [Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://iep.utm.edu/girard/), [Académie française](https://www.academie-francaise.fr/les-immortels/rene-girard)

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Thiel encountered Girard while studying philosophy at Stanford in the late 1980s and later participated in direct Girardian discussions and a reading group. Public sources commonly call Thiel Girard’s student, although the precise undergraduate course and enrollment details remain publicly unverified.
- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Thiel publicly interpreted and applied Girard’s ideas to competition, technology, politics, and Christianity; Girard supplied a favorable blurb for Thiel and David Sacks’s *The Diversity Myth*. Their crossing therefore went beyond passive influence into reciprocal public intellectual engagement.
- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Imitatio was launched in 2008 from conversations among Girard, Thiel, and Robert Hamerton-Kelly, with Thiel becoming a major patron of Girardian research and publication. This establishes repeated personal collaboration, not Girard’s endorsement of all Thiel’s later political positions. [Imitatio](https://www.imitatio.org/about-imitatio), [Stanford Graduate School of Business](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/case-studies/thiel-foundation-contrarian-philanthropy)

- **[T4]** **Documented fact:** Barthes participated in the October 1966 Johns Hopkins conference co-organized by Girard. The two occupied the same conference milieu, but the available evidence does not by itself establish friendship or a durable correspondence. [Johns Hopkins University](https://hub.jhu.edu/2018/08/08/rene-girard-evolution-desire/)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Girard engaged Freud throughout *Violence and the Sacred*, particularly *Totem and Taboo*, the Oedipus complex, parricide, incest prohibitions, and the primal horde. He credited Freud with approaching collective founding violence but argued that Freudian theory failed to recognize mimetic rivalry and the surrogate-victim mechanism. [Association Recherches Mimétiques bibliography](https://old.rene-girard.fr/57_p_44437/bibliographie.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Girard discussed Nijinsky in the closing movement of the filmed 2007 conversation *Le Sens de l’histoire*, alongside Proust and Stravinsky. No documentary evidence cited here indicates that Girard and Nijinsky ever met; Nijinsky died when Girard was twenty-six. [Association Recherches Mimétiques](https://old.rene-girard.fr/offres/gestion/events_57_oui-1/evenements-rene-girard-association-recherches-mimetiques.htmlhttp%3A/www.rene-girard.fr/offres/gestion/events_57_oui-1/evenements-rene-girard-association-recherches-mimetiques.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Girard treated Wagner together with Nietzsche in essays collected in *La Conversion de l’art*, including material on the “strategies of madness.” Wagner also figures in Girard’s late retrospective discussion of rivalry, culture, and European history. [Association Recherches Mimétiques](https://old.rene-girard.fr/offres/gestion/actus_57-1/les-actualites-rene-girard-association-recherches-mimetiques.html)
Girard participated in the 1966 Johns Hopkins structuralism conference where Derrida’s critique of Lévi-Strauss became prominent.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Thiel wrote extensively about Girard’s mimetic theory, scapegoating, revelation and apocalypse in “The Straussian Moment,” explicitly contrasting Girard with Nietzsche and Leo Strauss. [Essay text](https://www.vigneshatm.com/Compendia/2007-the-straussian-moment-thiel.pdf)
- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Thiel studied Girard’s work while an undergraduate at Stanford and later interacted with him personally, including at a small Stanford seminar organized by Thiel and Robert Hamerton-Kelly in 2004. Their relationship was that of student, intellectual patron and later interlocutor—not merely influence through books. [The New Yorker](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2011/11/28/no-death-no-taxes)

Wagner and Marx occupied the broader German revolutionary and exile milieu of 1848–49 without a documented meeting or correspondence.
D’Annunzio later made Wagner and Wagner’s association with Venice central subjects in Il fuoco.
Adorno later wrote a critical study of Wagner addressing commodity culture, myth, domination, orchestration, and regression.
Benjamin later engaged intellectually with the nineteenth-century cultural world of Wagnerian spectacle and aesthetic politics.
Satie later developed parody and anti-Wagnerian brevity in cultural reaction to French Wagnerism.
Stravinsky later attended Parsifal at Bayreuth and criticized the festival’s quasi-religious ritual.
Wagner’s mythic aesthetics later participated in a German Romantic intellectual inheritance in which Schelling was important.
Wagner later encountered Mozart’s life and music as part of his childhood musical education.
Wagner later drew on Shakespeare for Leubald and used his work as the basis of Das Liebesverbot.

- **[T1+]** **Documented fact:** Wagner repeatedly wrote about Mozart in his theoretical prose, including *Opera and Drama* (1851) and the 1860 “Letter on Music,” using Mozart’s operas to discuss the relationship between poet, drama, and composer. This is a substantial posthumous critical engagement, not a personal crossing. [Wagner text hosted by the University of Texas](https://www.laits.utexas.edu/wagner/selectedessays/pdf/Heise2.pdf), [“Lettre sur la musique”](https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Lettre_sur_la_musique_%28Richard_Wagner%29).
Proust later engaged Wagner's leitmotifs, operatic structures and music throughout the Recherche.
Dick discussed and defended the earlier composer Wagner and engaged with his music, myths, and political legacy.
Tolkien reportedly rejected simplistic comparisons between his Ring and Wagner’s, while scholars continue to debate possible indirect influence.
Serrano lectured about the earlier figure Wagner and incorporated Wagnerian myth, aesthetics, and symbolism into his system.
Duncan later danced to Wagner’s music and worked on the Tannhäuser Bacchanale at Bayreuth, connecting her to his music and institution after his death.
Lévi-Strauss credited Wagnerian leitmotifs and compositional transformations with shaping the organization of the Mythologiques.
Wagner based his opera Rienzi substantially on Bulwer's 1835 novel about Cola di Rienzo.
Laban later used Wagner's work as a connecting artistic object by staging the Tannhäuser Bacchanale and drawing on Wagnerian synthetic-theatre ideas.
Reuss worked in the Wagnerian professional milieu and may have sung in the 1882 Bayreuth Parsifal chorus, but his claimed personal relationship with Wagner is unproved.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Girard treated Wagner together with Nietzsche in essays collected in *La Conversion de l’art*, including material on the “strategies of madness.” Wagner also figures in Girard’s late retrospective discussion of rivalry, culture, and European history. [Association Recherches Mimétiques](https://old.rene-girard.fr/offres/gestion/actus_57-1/les-actualites-rene-girard-association-recherches-mimetiques.html)

text: Wagner and the Grimms drew on shared Germanic heroic and mythological source traditions, including the Nibelungenlied.
Cirlot discussed Wagner and Parsifal in a 1968 article connecting the work with Christianity and Buddhism.
Debussy, the later figure, wrote critically about Wagner and Wagnerism without ever meeting Wagner.
Engelmann wrote about Wagner in an 1883 publication and later performed excerpts from Wagner’s operas.
Diaghilev engaged indirectly with Wagner’s concept of integrated theatrical art as an artistic influence, although the two never met.
According to family recollection, the young Balanchine gained Tamara Geva's father's approval by playing Wagner's music at the piano.
Andersen met Wagner in Zürich in 1855, establishing an acquaintance without close collaboration.
Satie engaged with Wagner as the representative of a grandiose German musical model against which French modernists defined their aesthetic.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Kandinsky wrote about Wagner’s leitmotif as a musical means of creating a spiritual atmosphere around a character. Bakunin repeatedly met Wagner while both participated in the Dresden revolutionary movement of May 1849.
Lang’s Die Nibelungen and Wagner’s earlier Der Ring des Nibelungen separately transformed the shared Nibelung material.
Wagnerian ideas circulated in the Güell circle and have been linked to the program and symbolism of Park Güell, though some interpretations remain disputed.
Wagner is identified as a major cultural figure frequently central to Žižek's work.
Perrottet later choreographed dances for the Venus scene in a production of Wagner’s Tannhäuser.
Adam of Bremen later wrote about Rimbert and used works and materials associated with him in composing Book I of the Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum.
Ratramnus addressed Rimbert by name in a surviving letter that responded to Rimbert’s now-lost report and question about dog-headed peoples.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Amundsen wrote extensively about Scott’s earlier Antarctic expeditions, methods, planned route, and competing South Pole enterprise in *The South Pole* (1912). - **[T3]** **Documented fact:** From Madeira in October 1910, Amundsen sent Scott the telegram announcing that *Fram* was proceeding to Antarctica. At Polheim on 18 December 1911, he left Scott a directly addressed note asking him to forward Amundsen’s enclosed letter to King Haakon VII if the Norwegian party failed to return. Scott received and preserved both communications. [PBS, “Tragedy at the Pole”](https://www.pbs.org/wnet/secrets/tragedy-at-the-pole-background/7101/)
- **[T9+]** **Documented fact:** Amundsen’s party erected the Polheim tent at the South Pole in December 1911 and left records and letters inside it. Scott’s party reached the site on 17 January 1912, entered the tent, and took possession of the documents. The tent and its contents therefore passed between the two expeditions without Amundsen and Scott ever sharing the site.

[Amundsen’s *The South Pole*](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3414/pg3414-images.html)

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Amundsen met Mussolini at the Palazzo Diotti in Milan on 7 April 1924 while negotiating Italian participation and aircraft support for a projected Arctic flight. Museum documentation also records another meeting connected with the 1926 *Norge* expedition. [Roald Amundsen’s House, “The Plan 1925”](https://mia.no/roaldamundsen/en/the-plan-1925), [Fram Museum, *Norge* flight](https://frammuseum.no/polar-history/expeditions/the-norge-flight-1926/)
- **[T3]** **Documented fact:** Their engagement included written and contractual exchange: Amundsen and Mussolini signed the agreement governing the Italian airship’s participation in the *Norge* enterprise, while Mussolini also gave Amundsen a portrait bearing a personal inscription.
- **[T9-]** **Documented fact:** At their April 1924 Milan meeting, Mussolini presented Amundsen with the signed portrait. It remained at Amundsen’s Uranienborg home and is preserved as object RA 0662, making Amundsen the later recipient in this object-mediated connection. Scott and Shackleton exchanged letters disputing Shackleton’s planned use of McMurdo Sound for the Nimrod expedition.

Scott wrote Barrie a personal farewell letter while awaiting death in Antarctica in March 1912.
Conan Doyle corresponded directly with Scott about Scott’s candidacy for membership in Sheringham Golf Club.
Rodin reportedly attended the wedding of Kathleen Bruce and Scott at Hampton Court Palace in 1908.

Jackson and Finley were both listed in the founding leadership of the American Colonization Society in Washington, D.C., in December 1816, although Jackson was named without his consent and no personal collaboration is documented.
Finley followed Baldwin in the institutional history of Franklin College, later the University of Georgia, becoming president in 1817 after Baldwin’s earlier founding role and presidency.
Kepler and Fludd conducted a direct intellectual rivalry through published attacks and replies between 1619 and 1622.
Fludd drew on and transformed the earlier writings of Paracelsus concerning chemical medicine, macrocosm–microcosm relations, and Galenic authority.
Fludd inherited ideas from Agrippa's earlier writings on occult philosophy.
Fludd inherited elements of the Christian Cabalistic tradition associated with Pico.
Reuchlin's earlier Christian Cabalistic writings formed part of Fludd's source tradition.
Fludd reportedly drew from an intellectual environment shaped by Trithemius's writings on learned magic and cryptic or angelic knowledge.
Fludd's ideas about divine unity, infinity, and creation drew partly on the earlier Cusan tradition.
Fludd's encyclopedic project reportedly drew from earlier Lullian traditions of combinatory thought and universal knowledge.
Fludd wrote in defense of literature centered on the possibly mythical Christian Rosenkreuz.
Kircher's later intellectual projects inherited and sometimes contested a field of encyclopedic, musical, magnetic, and hieroglyphic inquiry associated with Fludd.
Jung's later work incorporated Fludd's images and the Kepler–Fludd controversy into his interpretation of alchemical and intellectual history.
Pauli later examined the Kepler–Fludd polemic as emblematic of a division between quantitative and symbolic knowledge.
Yates's scholarship made Fludd central to modern accounts of Renaissance memory, Hermeticism, theater, and Rosicrucian culture.

Hooke discussed Aristotle’s account of animals inhabiting sponge cavities, treating it as compatible with his observations while calling for further investigation.
Hooke praised Copernicus as an exemplary discoverer and later sought observational evidence for Earth’s annual motion in the Copernican system.
Hooke praised Galileo’s telescopic discoveries and compared Galileo’s chart of 36 Pleiades stars with his own observation of 78.
Hooke examined and rejected Kepler’s explanation of the atmospheric penumbra and later treated Keplerian planetary motion as requiring a mechanical cause.
Hooke critically discussed Descartes’s vortex theory of gravity, arguing that lunar gravity and motion created difficulties for it.
Hooke and Huygens engaged through correspondence, reports, and publications about pendulums, spring-controlled watches, astronomy, optics, and competing priority claims.
Locke wrote directly to Hooke in October 1678, establishing a documented epistolary connection.
Leibniz attended Royal Society meetings involving Hooke and later exchanged letters with him, including correspondence about geographical surveys.
Hooke and Newton exchanged substantive correspondence about optics and planetary motion, including Hooke’s proposals concerning central attraction and inverse-square dependence.
Hooke and Newton met through Royal Society activities in London and became adversarial institutional colleagues over optics and gravitational priority.
Hooke corresponded directly with Halley about comet observations and other notices, while Halley later conveyed messages between Hooke and Newton.
Hooke and Halley worked together in the Royal Society milieu and personally discussed planetary dynamics with Christopher Wren in January 1684.
Huygens encountered Hooke in the Royal Society milieu during his English visits, although they are not documented as close friends.
Robert Maxwell was Ghislaine Maxwell’s father, employer-associated social companion, and especially close parent.
Epstein attended a memorial event after Robert Maxwell’s death and may previously have encountered him in New York social or financial settings.
Robert Maxwell acquired in 1986 the yacht later called Lady Ghislaine, which had been constructed or commissioned within the Khashoggi family orbit.
Robert Maxwell and Trump were placed in overlapping New York yacht, newspaper, and social settings around 1989–91, without evidence of a close partnership.
After Robert Maxwell’s death, Lombardi diagrammed international financial and political networks in which the Maxwell affair was emblematic.

- **[T9-]** **Documented fact.** Central Park is the shared site. Vaux and Frederick Law Olmsted originated its winning Greensward design in 1858; Moses, as parks commissioner from 1934 to 1960, subsequently administered and materially altered the inherited landscape, adding nineteen playgrounds, athletic facilities, Wollman Rink, and other recreational works. Vaux died in 1895, so this is a site-mediated succession, not a personal encounter. [Central Park Conservancy](https://www.centralparknyc.org/articles/central-park-history)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** The Robert Moses Papers contain correspondence with David Rockefeller concerning the financing and construction of the United Nations headquarters in **1949**, further correspondence in **1959**, and a David Rockefeller file from **1979** concerning proposed updates to East River waterfront parks and playgrounds. The record establishes sustained written engagement on New York development matters, not merely membership in overlapping civic circles. [NYPL finding aid](https://archives.nypl.org/mss/2071)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** Moses and Wright exchanged correspondence over many years. The Robert Moses Papers identify exchanges in **1943**, correspondence and texts of talks associated with Princeton’s bicentennial in **1946–47**, and further correspondence in **1949 and 1952–58**. The 1959 files include Moses’s correspondence with Wright and, after Wright’s death that April, with his widow concerning the opening of the Guggenheim Museum. [NYPL finding aid](https://archives.nypl.org/mss/2071)

- **[T9-]** **Documented fact.** Central Park passed from the nineteenth-century design legacy of Olmsted and Calvert Vaux to Moses’s twentieth-century parks administration. Olmsted and Vaux’s Greensward plan became the basis of the park beginning in **1858**; during **1934–60**, Moses’s department inserted playgrounds, ballfields, handball courts, Wollman Rink, and other facilities into that inherited landscape. Olmsted died in 1903, before Moses entered park administration, so no personal meeting is implied. [Central Park Conservancy](https://www.centralparknyc.org/articles/central-park-history)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** Moses’s papers contain correspondence with George H. W. Bush in the **1971–72** general files, during Bush’s service as United States ambassador to the United Nations. The folder-level description establishes written contact but does not disclose enough content to characterize its subject or closeness. [NYPL finding aid](https://archives.nypl.org/mss/2071)

- **[T3]** **Documented fact.** Moses’s archive records a letter to Kennedy in **1957** and correspondence with him in **1958**. As president, Kennedy also wrote directly to Moses on **5 October 1961** about federal participation in the proposed New York World’s Fair. [NYPL finding aid](https://archives.nypl.org/mss/2071); [American Presidency Project](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/letters-mayor-wagner-and-robert-moses-concerning-the-new-york-worlds-fair)
- **[T5]** **Documented fact.** Kennedy and Moses appeared together during the federal-pavilion dedication and inspection of the World’s Fair site in New York on **14 December 1962**. Contemporary photographic documentation shows them inspecting the fair model, and surviving film records Kennedy at the dedication with Moses acting as fair president. [New York World’s Fair records](https://nyplorg-data-archives.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/collection/pdf_finding_aid/nywf64.pdf)

- **[T5]** **Documented fact.** Kennedy and Moses appeared together during the federal-pavilion dedication and inspection of the World’s Fair site in New York on **14 December 1962**. - **[T3]** **Documented fact.** Senator Prescott Bush sent Moses congratulations after Moses received a General Motors highway award in **1953**, and the archive preserves additional correspondence between them from **1958**. The surviving finding-aid descriptions establish direct written exchange but do not justify inferring friendship or a broader political alliance. [NYPL finding aid](https://archives.nypl.org/mss/2071)

- **[T5]** **Documented fact.** Moses visited Walt Disney’s California studio in **April 1962** to inspect attractions being developed for the 1964–65 New York World’s Fair. Disney personally showed him the prototype Audio-Animatronic Abraham Lincoln; Moses then pressed for its inclusion in the fair, helping produce Illinois’s *Great Moments with Mr. Lincoln* pavilion. Disney later hosted Moses again during a **1963** studio visit, and the two appeared together at the pavilion announcement in New York. This was a direct working relationship involving repeated meetings, not merely parallel participation in the fair. [Disney D23 history](https://d23.com/the-hall-of-presidents-story/); [Disney archival magazine](https://disneyvacationclub.disney.go.com/media/dvc/languagespecific/eng/member/justformembers/disneyfilesmagazine/2009/DisneyFilesMagazine_Fall2009.pdf)
Oppenheimer and Einstein met and conversed at Princeton about physics, government, and Oppenheimer’s security troubles.
Oppenheimer met Bohr in European physics circles and later discussed nuclear design and policy with him at Los Alamos.
Oppenheimer and Fermi worked together through the Manhattan Project and the Interim Committee’s Scientific Panel.
Oppenheimer met Dirac in the European quantum-mechanics community of the late 1920s.
Oppenheimer and Schrödinger belonged to the same international theoretical-physics milieu, with Schrödinger’s wave mechanics shaping Oppenheimer’s field.
Oppenheimer encountered Heisenberg within the Göttingen-centered quantum-physics network.
Oppenheimer worked in Pauli’s Zürich intellectual circle and later exchanged scientific correspondence with him.
Von Neumann consulted under Oppenheimer’s Los Alamos leadership and later supported him during the 1954 security proceeding.
Feynman worked under Oppenheimer at Los Alamos and subsequently received mentorship and professional advocacy from him.
Kennedy approved the Enrico Fermi Award that Oppenheimer was scheduled to receive in 1963, although Kennedy died before its presentation.
Kennedy selected Oppenheimer for the 1963 Enrico Fermi Award as a symbolic rehabilitation but died before presenting it.
Weizmann met Oppenheimer at Princeton in 1947 and discussed the possibility of building a nuclear reactor in the Yishuv.
Pauli and Oppenheimer overlapped in the Princeton-era American theoretical-physics milieu without an established close partnership.
Karp invoked the Manhattan Project associated with Oppenheimer as a model for national technological mobilization.
Skyrme worked at Los Alamos under the institutional authority of its director, Oppenheimer, although no personal interaction was established.
Einstein and Oppenheimer shared the Institute for Advanced Study environment at Princeton, where Einstein supported and advised Oppenheimer during his security controversy.

- **[T5]** **Documented fact:** Ben-Gurion met Oppenheimer during the physicist’s 1958 visit to Israel for the opening of the Weizmann Institute’s nuclear-science facility. Ben-Gurion subsequently reported their conversation to the Israeli cabinet, including their discussion of nuclear war and Israel’s national purpose. [Martin Kramer’s documentary reconstruction](https://martinkramer.org/2024/01/10/oppenheimer-on-israel/), [Forward account](https://forward.com/news/556495/the-time-oppenheimer-met-ben-gurion-to-discuss-israels-nuclear-quest/)
- **[T5]** **Reported fact, with a disputed embellishment:** A separate 1955 Ben-Gurion letter also says that he met Oppenheimer during an Israeli visit. Ben-Gurion publicly recalled meetings with both Einstein and Oppenheimer in 1961. Claims that Oppenheimer and Edward Teller jointly advised Ben-Gurion in Tel Aviv in 1952 about plutonium production are poorly sourced and conflict with evidence that Teller’s first Israeli visit occurred later; that stronger nuclear-advisory story should not be treated as established. [Contemporary JTA report](https://www.jta.org/archive/ben-gurion-renews-call-to-u-s-jewish-youth-to-settle-in-israel), [source-critical review](https://jewishjournal.com/commentary/opinion/379502/did-j-robert-oppenheimer-help-israel-build-the-bomb/)
Witten joined the Institute for Advanced Study after Oppenheimer’s earlier tenure there as director, with no personal connection documented.
Oppenheimer attended the Ethical Culture School that Adler had founded and continued to guide.

Roger Bacon taught and commented on Aristotle while critically engaging his translations and scholastic interpretation.
Roger Bacon engaged Plato indirectly through Latin traditions and authorities that influenced the organization of his later philosophy.
Roger Bacon engaged Augustine as an authority in his theological, philosophical, and linguistic writings.
Roger Bacon and Albertus Magnus occupied the Parisian intellectual milieu and worked on overlapping philosophical materials during the mid-thirteenth century.
Roger Bacon and Thomas Aquinas participated in overlapping Parisian debates about Aristotle, astrology, theology, and the intellect.
Roger Bacon later entered the religious order founded by Francis of Assisi and worked within its institutional and reform traditions.
Francis Bacon later wrote about Roger Bacon as an exceptional schoolman who investigated nature's mechanical secrets.
Roger Bacon's geographical calculations entered a textual tradition later available to proponents of westward travel associated with Christopher Columbus.
Roger Bacon's authentic and attributed works later circulated within the English learned culture in which John Dee participated.
Roger Bacon and Ramon Llull were posthumously connected through pseudo-alchemical corpora and later publications that juxtaposed their names.

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact.** In *Sacred Mysteries* (1886), Le Plongeon quoted Roger Bacon on withholding philosophical discoveries from the unworthy and discussed Bacon’s learning and imprisonment as part of a history of esoteric secrecy. [Primary text](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/57458/57458-h/57458-h.htm)

- **[T1-]** *Etidorhpa* gives Roger Bacon unusually sustained treatment: Lloyd praised his intellect, recounted his imprisonment and Hermetic beliefs, described his claims about alchemical gold and predictive mirrors, and quoted his anticipation of rapidly moving horseless vehicles. **Documented fact.** [Primary text](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/37775/pg37775-images.html)

- **[T1-]** **Documented fact:** Agrippa cited and discussed works attributed to Roger Bacon in constructing his accounts of magic, mathematics, optics, experimental arts, and occult properties.
